q: What is the Goal of life?
What is religion?
a: Swami Vivekananda tells us: --
" Each soul is potentially divine.
" The Goal is to manifest this Divinity within, by controlling nature, external and internal.
" Do this either by work, or worship, or psychic control, or philosophy -- by one or more or all of these and be free.
" This is the whole of religion. Doctrines, or dogmas, or rituals, or books, or temples, or forms are but secondary details."
(a) When we try to understand the first of these 4 aphorisms, we find that
(i) The truth applies to ‘each’ one of us without any exception whatsoever, irrespective of caste, creed, gender etc. etc.
(ii) Each living being is called a ‘soul’ because it is basically of the nature of ‘awareness’ working in a particular body-mind set up which is like an external covering.

(iii) What we see now is not our real nature. Today our senses are continuously interacting with the objects outside and our mind is very restless and hence our real nature -- the pure, perfect, blissful awareness -- is hidden -- covered as it were. We will have to go very very deep within ourselves to find out what we really are. And yet that being our very nature, it is never really lost, and hence it is termed as ‘potential’. It is really Infinite.

(iv) The great sages, whose vision is not obstructed by the outside appearances, clearly see that One Infinite Universal Existence-Consciousness-Bliss Absolute with Infinite Power and Perfection present in every individual hidden by the individual’s limited thoughts feelings and actions etc.

(b) Hence, as the goal of each seed is to evolve into a fully grownup tree -- mango-seed into mango tree, apple-seed into apple tree, so the ‘goal’ of each individual being is the manifestation of the Divine within in his/her own way. What obstructs this manifestation? The ‘nature’ of our body-mind set up. This has to be properly ‘attuned’ to our Reality -- our divine potential within.

(c) Each individual finds itself to be finite, limited, imperfect and has several wants and desires and is acted upon by everything of the outside world -- is pulled and dragged by his desires, wants and imperfections. All these are his/her bondages. Finally when the Infinite Divinity manifests itself in the individual he/she finds himself/herself free from all limitations, bondages, imperfection, drags and desires. This is called Freedom (Moksha) and is another way of looking at the ‘Goal’. For this, we have to properly use whatever faculties we possess, after learning the secrets of work, worship, psychic control and philosophy.

(d) Thus in the first aphorism Swami Vivekananda has revealed the fundamental Truth. In the second he has pointed out the Goal as the natural corollary of this truth. In the third he has shown all possible methods to achieve it and also given the impetus to ‘do it’. These three together constitute ‘the whole of religion’ says the Swami.

(e) Of course the same Religion can be thought of in various other ways. "Religion is realization" -- says the great Swami over and over again. Let us try to understand what it means. When we analyze our lives and the world around us philosophically, we come to the conclusion that the Ultimate Truth is one universal Reality, which we generally call God. But when we consider our ordinary, superficial experience of the world we do not see ‘God’ at all. God is thus the ultimate Truth though it is not a fact of our experience today. But by proper struggle this ultimate Truth has to become the permanent fact of experience, then only we can say that it has become ‘real’ to us now. This is called ‘real-isation’ of Truth -- and this is religion.

q: What should be the basic guidelines of life?
a: 1. Conviction of one’s own and others potential divinity should be the first principle.
2. Faith in oneself, which directly follows from the above conviction.

3. The four cardinal virtues: i. Unselfishness; ii. Deep devotion to God, the Universal Infinite, worshipped in any form or manner; iii. Self-control; IV. Rational understanding of the ultimate nature of things.
4. Devotion to Duty
5. Regularity of spiritual practice.
6. Planned and disciplined life.
7. Zest for knowledge.
8. Following everything that makes oneself strong physically, mentally, morally, spiritually, and avoiding everything which weakens.
9. If one is cent per cent sure about a thing being right, one must have the courage to follow it.
These are a few points.
10. The passage from Trattoria Upanishad which was read on the occasion of valedictory contains beautiful guidelines.

Having taught the Vedas, the preceptor imparts this post-instruction to the students: "Speak the truth. Practice righteousness. Make no mistake about study. Having offered the desirable wealth to the teacher, do not cut off the line of progeny. There should be no inadvertence about truth. There should be no deviation from righteous activity. There should be no error about protection of you. Do not neglect propitious activities. Do not be careless about learning and teaching. There should be no error in the duties towards the gods and manes. Let your mother be a goddess unto you. Let your father be a god unto you. Let your teacher be a god unto you. Let your guest be a god unto you. The works that are not blameworthy are to be resorted to, but not the others. Those actions of ours that are commendable are to be followed by you, but not the others. You should, by offering seats, remove the fatigue of those learned virtuous people who are more praiseworthy among us. The offering should be with honor; the offering should not be with dishonor. The offering should be in plenty. The offering should be with modesty. The offering should be with awe. The offering should be with sympathy. Then, should you have any doubt with regard to duties or customs, you should behave in those matters just as the learned virtuous people do, who may happen to be there and who are able deliberators, who are adepts in those duties and customs, who are not directed by others, who are not cruel, and who are desirous of merit. Then as for the accused people, you should behave with regard to them just as the learned virtuous people do, who may happen to be there and who are able deliberators, who are adepts in those duties and customs, who are not directed by others, who are not cruel, and who are desirous of merit.

q: Which yoga should students follow?
Is meditation and long prayers, the only way to reach God?
What should the children do whose first and primary Goal is to study?
a: We must first know what yoga is and what the different yogas are. Let us recapitulate the answers to Q.1 and Q.2 in which we quoted Swami Vivekananda: "(i) Each soul is potentially divine; (ii) The goal is to manifest this DIVINITY within by controlling nature, external and internal; (iii) Do this either by work, or worship, or psychic control, or philosophy -- by one, or more, or all of these and be free. (iv) This is the whole of religion. Doctrines, or dogmas, or rituals, or books, or temples, or forms are but secondary details."

In another place Swami Vivekananda says -- "Our main problem is to be free. It is evident then that until we realize ourselves as the Absolute, we cannot attain deliverance (liberation). Yet there are various ways of attaining this realization. These methods have the generic name of yoga (to join, to join ourselves to our reality). These yogas, though divided into various groups, can principally be classed into four; and as each is only a method leading indirectly to the realization of the Absolute, they are suited to different temperaments." (C.W.8, 152) Let us try to understand what are these ‘temperaments’ to which these yogas are suitable. According to Western psychologists, the human mind has three distinct functions, viz., ‘thinking’, ‘feeling’ and ‘will’. Let us consider ‘will’. "I shall do" (such and such a thing) is an expression of the will, and "I shall not do" (such and such a thing) is also an expression -- but they are of quite opposite nature. Hence the last one can be called as a separate function of the mind -- the fourth -- and named as self-check or self-control or self-discipline. In each individual these four faculties are present in different degrees and their varying percentages/proportions lead to infinite number of ‘temperaments’. Add to these the variety in details within each of these functions, e.g., fatherly love, motherly love, brotherly love, etc. etc. -- there is no limit to the variation in individual temperaments. This makes for an infinite approaches towards ‘controlling nature -- external and internal’ so that the ‘Divine within’ may ‘manifest ’. For each person has to start from where he or she is -- change the direction of the different faculties which are present in him/her towards ‘infinity’ -- and to achieve this he or she also has to use whatever faculties he or she possesses in whatever degree. For example in the chapter ending colophons of the Gita we find the mention of 18 yogas starting from ‘Arjuna Vishada Yoga’, ‘Sankhya Yoga’ and so on.

However if we have to ‘understand’ the processes involved in changing the orientation of a particular faculty and also how to use any of the particular faculties -- we shall have to study them ‘separately’ though in actual life they would always be mixed and overlapping. This led Swami Vivekananda and other thinkers to show the path by grouping under four broad categories of Karma Yoga, Bhakti yoga, Raja Yoga and Jnana Yoga dealing respectively with the faculties of will, feeling, self-control and thinking.

This will help us to understand what yoga ‘we’ should follow. If we are students, we have to ‘study’ which no doubt becomes a part of our life and our primary concern. But that cannot define the whole of our life or our Goal or even ‘the path towards the goal’ for which we will have to analyze our own personalities with the help of wise people to find out what are the faculties and potentials we possess and how to harness them and how to improve them etc. Thus we can have a more active student, a more feeling student, a more disciplined student, a more intelligent student etc. though we should always try to develop ourselves harmoniously with respect to all these four faculties. And do you not know that Education itself also is not defined merely as ‘studies’ but as physical, mental and moral ‘training’ wherein ‘mental’ training includes training of thinking, feeling, will and self-control etc.
Now let us think of ‘studies’ and the various motivations etc. involved in it.

I was once amidst students of the higher secondary (11th & 12th standard) classes who told me that their parents enjoyed watching T.V. but did not allow them to do so and told them -- "Now you go on studying so that later on you can enjoy these pleasures." They then asked me (I don’t know whether they asked the same question to their parents or not) -- "Why should we not enjoy pleasures now itself? What would happen if we die tomorrow?" I exclaimed -- "Alas! How wrong to motivate towards study by telling that it would give them the route passage (through money?) for the enjoyment of pleasures (which a pig can do best without any education)! Why not tell them that the process of education will help them become well developed individuals by increasing their power of thinking, the capacity of understanding the world and themselves better and better, and by giving them the ability to work in different fields of human endeavor and express their respective potentials fully and properly. Side by side they should develop their physical abilities and skills, develop their feelings in the right direction and learn to control passions and self-destructive emotions etc. They should become wiser and wiser and abler and abler. On the other hand indulging in fleeting pleasures of the senses which titillate (the nerves) and fritter away their energy will hamper their capacity to improve. If we run after enjoyments, we shall not have the power to improve ourselves and those enjoyments will also slip away from us like shadows, but if we continually struggle for self-improvement then happiness will follow us. Of course, we must have some enjoyments or pleasures in a planned and disciplined way so that we become ‘re-freshed’ when we are fatigued by the constant struggle for improvement and that is why these types of activities are called ‘recreation’ which is an essential part of the science of struggle for improvement which is called ‘education’. And of course we can derive abundant pleasures from creative cultural activities, along with games and sports and useful hobbies. So we find some students engaged in ‘meditation and long prayers’ and yet coming up very well in their studies and some others using meditation and ‘short’ prayers to improve their power of self-discipline, peace of mind and concentration so that they do their studies easily and successfully. It all depends on individual ‘temperament’, but the important point is to be aware of the Goal of life which is not only to be a really well-developed man or woman in whom all available faculties are properly used and groomed, but also to go towards becoming like God.

q: Does one have to think of the society every time he wants to do something?
a: There are two basic tendencies in the human mind -- the lure of enjoyment and the struggle for improvement. These are also called the pull of the ‘pleasurable’ and the pull of the ‘ultimately beneficial’. If the first pull is left unchecked it leads to ultimate ruination, while the second pull or struggle if checked will stagnate our life. Thinking of society is useful to check the downslide of life resulting from the first temptation. On the other hand, if one is absolutely sure that one is trying to improve oneself then he/she should not allow himself/herself to be checked by society. It is of course always useful to get one’s course of action approved by some really wise person.

q: What is the importance of good behavior?
Is culture to be shown to everyone or it is enough if we have it in us?
a: We must first understand the subtle difference between character and conduct or behavior. Character is what we really are ourselves and conduct is how we appear to others.

If character is perfect it reflects in good behavior. Otherwise good behavior can also be a ‘mask’. In any case the effect of good behavior is that others become pleased. The effect on ourselves varies -- (i) If it is an expression of good character, then good behavior strengthens it.
(ii) If behavior is only a mask, then it may make our life artificial.

Similarly, if we really have the culture in us, it will come out even in our dealing with others. Hence if it is not coming out in that manner, we should know that we do not have it fully developed in us as yet, and hence we must strive hard to develop it more and more on the inside. On the other hand if we try to show or are merely taught to show culture to everyone without really having it in ourselves, we are likely to turn into hypocrites and will never be at ease with ourselves nor with others.

q: What is a friend? Why does the human heart wish to have a friend?
Please give guidelines for being a friend.
a: This is an extremely important question in actual life of any individual human being.
(a) ‘A friend in need is a friend indeed’ is the old proverb.

(b) Really ‘God’ alone is our best friend. The great sage Shankaracharya says that a ‘friend’ is a ‘friend’ usually only so long as we are nice to him, but God is our friend always and ever. (Commentary on Gita 9,18)

(c) This God, who is the Ultimate Reality -- One only, without a second -- manifests Himself in innumerably unique ways through the infinite variety of human beings created by Him out of Himself. This leads to a situation where each individual finds himself/herself different from others, separate from others, limited, and hence, to complete himself/herself, he/she craves for a friend who is an expression of the same common Reality and yet is differently constituted. So much so that many of us feel totally at a loss to cope up with life without a proper friend or friends.

(d) If we can be always aware that friendship is based on two factors -- variety outside, and yet sharing the common background and support of same Universal Reality called God so that the third friend God is always available in case of our falling out with each other due to misunderstandings etc. -- we can be true friends always.

(e) The purpose of friendship is to compliment and supplement each other and help each other to strive for perfection. When perfection is reached we are not in need of anyone to help us, and then we can be real friends because we really feel the same God in us and in others.
(f) Friendship should be based on giving and not expecting.
(g) Friendship should lead to more and more improvement together. It should never be against anybody and never lead to common disaster by doing anything bad together!
(h) Friendship is destroyed by imposing and expecting. It is really built up in freedom.
(i) Select your friends very carefully in such a way that every merit in you gets a boost and not the demerits or evil passions.
(j) Friendship is sustained by each one struggling to be a better and better individual and by always helping each other.

q: From where do we come and where do we go?
a: There is the following scene in the life of Bhagavan Buddha. His father, King Shuddhodan, had made such arrangements that no kind of unhappiness could cast its shadow on the life of the prince. One day he was seated in his royal chamber along with his beautiful and worthy wife Yashodhara and charming young son Rahul. Music and dance surrounded them. At such a moment some angels appeared to float in the space above, moving from one side to the other (or were they forms taken by his own higher thoughts?). They were singing a song with the following refrain:-
"From where we come, -- we do not know!
To where we go from here, -- we do not know!
Drifting, drifting, drifting, -- all the time.
We yearn for rest and peace, -- but we get neither rest nor peace! Drifting, drifting, drifting, -- all the time.
From where we come, -- we do not know.
To where we go from here, -- we do not know!"

And then he got the ‘awakening’ that unless one knows the truth, -- the meaning and the purpose of life, -- all pleasures etc. make one more and more blind. Hence before we can answer this let us turn to some more fundamental questions.

q: Why is man born? [Why do we live?]
a: (i) It was a few years back that a girl student of I yr. B.E. (Electronics) told me that she found absolutely no meaning in life. "Life is certainly a vacuum" she said. "Whatever meaning we try to find in life can be proved to be zero, a mere nothing." On being asked the ‘history of her thoughts’ she stated -- "When I was in the 9th standard I thought only of one thing -- my aim of becoming an electronic engineer. Mathematics and Science subjects were to my liking; I studied hard, had a good percentage of marks in 12th, secured admission in the Engineering College and got the branch of my choice. I scored good marks in 1st year engineering examination also. So I thought my aim of becoming Electronic Engineer was almost fulfilled -- as it was only a matter of time. It was at this point that it struck me that this ‘becoming an electronic engineer’ is absolutely ‘nothing’ and then I thought about everything that people find worthwhile and I found all of it was absolutely nothing. This is then my thought that there is no ‘meaning’ in this ‘life’ -- it is a vacuum.”

(ii) After a few days another person -- a lady of around 35 years of age came to the Ashrama and asked whether we teach ‘meditation’. On being asked what made her enquire about it, she said -- "I completed my studies, went into a job, got married and had children -- all this happened like a flow. Then I faced struggle on all fronts. But now the job as well as the married life has become smooth and the children are growing nicely. (The necessary struggles brought about by the flow of life are thus over.) And at this point I am struck with the feeling that life is a
vacuum. I now realize that I don’t know ‘why’ I liv e? I have heard that meditation may help me to find out the ‘why’ of living life."

(iii) Since then several people at different stages of life -- boys studying in Engineering colleges -- even a girl studying in 8th standard have been asking the same question over and over again -- why do we live? Has life any meaning or is all this just a vacuum. Some boys have even told their parents that the ‘meaning’ which they (the parents) find in life is nothing but a subjective projection of their own, while life itself does not appear to have any meaning.

(iv) I told all of them that (a) what they think is correct to an extent; (b) this can be called ‘awakening’; (c) but there is another side to it also. The reason why we feel this futility etc. is that we are dealing with mere shadows in this world. But shadows always indicate the ‘thing’ of which they are shadows. If we can get a hold over that ‘thing’, then alone and surely this feeling of emptiness would vanish.

(v) This ‘thing’ of which this world is a shadow - - is called God -- the Absolute and ultimate Reality. Let us turn our attention then to understand what is this God, to find the meaning and purpose of life.

q: Is there a God or is it a supernatural power?
a: It is a wonderful question and let us first try to understand the mind of the questioner who asked it. [Many people think God to be just a supernatural power while this question has put these in two separate categories.]

When we look at this infinite world around us and try to think rationally about its origin and also about its actual running -- our sense of cause and effect will not allow us to feel satisfied with the idea that the world is functioning by itself or automatically etc. Either there is a supernatural power which is the cause of all this or there is a Conscious Entity called God. Now, if the ‘supernatural power’ is an unconscious force like ‘Electricity’ etc. how can it rule, govern, direct or be the cause of the running of this world? Not only has it to be a conscious entity, but It has to be Infinite Consciousness having infinite power. Some people try to disbelieve the existence of such Infinity of consciousness and power. That reminds us of a story of an able-bodied military man who wanted some excuse to quit the military. He decided to pretend having lost the range of his vision. He went to his captain on the field and told him that his vision was impaired. When he was asked to explain he said -- "Sir, you see that tree beyond this field of ours with that nail on it. Well I can’t see that nail." The Captain looked in that direction but could not even see the tree! So it was proved that the soldier had a sharper vision as both the tree and the nail on it were visible to him. Similarly, when anyone tries to disprove the existence of God -- he holds on to some idea of God which he tries not to accept!

Of course all our ideas of God are hazy in the beginning as we are overpowered by the His creation and are lost in it. Let us start with this basic logical necessity of an Infinite Consciousness with ultimate power ruling the universe and come to terms with clearer and clearer view of this GOD.

q: Is it really God who constructs us?
How was the world made?
How does God spread his powers?
If we say that God is one, then why aren’t people one?
How can we believe in God?
How did God come into the world?
How do we believe that God exists?
a: In order to understand these things let us take the help of the scriptures. The Vedas are known to be the oldest scriptures in the world and the portion of these Vedas which deals with ultimate knowledge is called the Vedanta or also as the Upanishads. The sixth chapter of the Chhandogya Upanishad relates this anecdote -

Shvetaketu returned to his house at the age of 24 when he thought he had completed his education. He appeared conceited, proud of his learning and immodest. His father, -- a great sage, asked him, "Did you ask for that instruction by which even the unknown becomes known?" On being asked by Shvetaketu to illustrate what he meant, the father said -- "By knowing a lump of clay in reality, everything made of clay is known -- as the product is only a name and a form of the clay which alone is real (in this illustration). Similarly for things made of Gold or Iron. Such is the instruction about the Reality of this entire world." Shvetaketu then requested his father to give him that special instruction. His father said that in order to know who made us or how we were made or how the world was made etc. we must first of all try to think of the situation before the world was created and before we were created. We shall immediately find that then there was an Absolute Existence, one alone without a second. We must also remember that all this that we see now including ourselves was absolutely non-existent then. There was non-existence alone. But our sense of cause-effect will not allow us to think that anything can come out of ‘nothing’. Hence we have to think of the starting point as the Infinite Absolute Existence – One, without a second. (This is how we believe in God.) And again for this to come out of ‘that’, ‘that’ has to be not only Absolute Existence, but Absolute Consciousness also – One, without a second (this is how we believe in God) and ‘that’ Absolute Consciousness-Existence ‘willed’ -- ‘I am one: I shall be many: Let me take the forms of separate individuals.’(That is why though God is one, we are many.) From It [It is remarkable that God is not called ‘He’ or ‘She’ by the Upanishads because such difference of gender cannot exist in the Infinite Absolute Ultimate Reality] then came out space, air, light, water, solids -- the different bodies -- and in each body the absolute consciousness reflected itself as the individual consciousness. (That is how God spread His powers and came into this world!)

Let us try to further answer the last question, "How can we believe in God?" In the above passage of Chhandogya Upanishad and similar passages from other Upanishads God is understood as the ultimate Absolute Existence-Consciousness-Bliss from which this world takes form, because of whom the world appears to have some sort of stability in spite of the continuous changes going on and in whom it returns again and again.

Now let us try to understand what we are and what God is in relation to us -- the living beings. Let us take the example of a dark room getting illumined when we switch on an electric bulb inside. Without the luminous bulb neither the room nor any objects in the room could be cognized. We immediately conclude that the bulb is the source of light for the room and the objects contained therein. Now look at the bulb. We shall see that the whole bulb is not really the source of light nor is it self-luminous. The source of the light is the heated filament which is self-luminous due to its heat. The bulb has a cover with a shape to make it appear separate from the room and the air has been removed etc. from the space enclosed by it, differentiating it from outside and hence it is filled with the ‘glow’ of the light emanating from the filament. Now let us apply this illustration to ourselves.

We have our ‘consciousness’ which illumines our mind and body and the entire universe for us, and this ‘consciousness of ours’ is like the separated glow of the ‘Consciousness-in-itself’ which we call God.

Swami Vivekananda gives an illustration: A gigantic engine is running on a track and a small ant sitting on the rails climbs down to save itself. What is the difference! The mighty ‘engine’ is not ‘aware’ of itself or of the ant, while the ant is ‘aware’ of itself and also of the engine (and hence tries to save itself from the engine). The difference between dull matter and living beings is therefore this ‘awareness’ and not merely the fact of breathing or any metabolical process. We know ourselves and the world because of this awareness. We really are this ‘awareness’. Now try to look at this awareness and we shall find it to be a reflection or a limited form of appearance (like the glow in the bulb) of THE Awareness-in-itself. This Absolute Awareness -- one without a Second is called God. (Like the heat and light which shine through the heated filament and express themselves through the bulb). That is why one girl when asked for proof of God replied, "The very fact that ‘I’ exist and I am aware of my existence has been possible only because God exists as the Absolute Ultimate Existence-Consciousness."

Let us analytically understand one more vital fact pertaining to our ‘knowledge’. Swami Vivekananda explains: "The mind must always travel between two extremes. You can think of limited space, but that very idea also gives you unlimited space. Close your eyes and think of a little space; at the same time you perceive the little circle, you have a circle round it of unlimited dimensions. It is the same with time. Try to think of a second; you will have, with the same act of perception, to think of time which is unlimited. So is it with knowledge. Knowledge is only a germ in man, but you will have to think of infinite knowledge around it, so that the very constitution of our mind shows us that there is unlimited knowledge, and the yogis call that unlimited knowledge God. ... in thinking of the limited, the mind must think of the unlimited; and that if one part of that perception is true, so also must the other be, for the reason that their value as perceptions of the mind is equal. The very fact that man has a little knowledge, shows that God has unlimited knowledge. If I am to take one, why not the other? Reason forces me to take both or reject both. If I believe that there is a man with a little knowledge, I must also admit that there is someone behind him with unlimited knowledge." (Raja Yoga P.139, 140-41)
So on both sides -- universal and individual -- God is the basis of all existence, activity and awareness. Not to understand this is blindness, foolishness and superficiality of life.

q: What is there in God that we call him God?
a: This question asks us to ‘define’ God. Let us try.
(a) We have already seen that God is Absolute Infinite Undivided Eternal Existence- Consciousness-Bliss (Sat-chit-Ananda).
(b) God is both the efficient and material cause of creation (or projection or appearance), preservation (or sustenance or continuation) and dissolution (or disappearance) of the world.

[When a potter makes a pot from clay, he is said to be the efficient cause of the pot while clay is the material cause. In case of the world, God is both the efficient and material cause, i.e. God projects the world from within himself by his own will.]
(c) God is the one Ruler of this universe (nobody has the power to overrule him).
(d) God is eternally pure, All-pervading, Ever-free, Almighty, All-knowing, All-merciful, Teacher of all teachers.
(e) God is inexpressible LOVE and BLISS.
(f) God is Absolutely Perfect. God is the repository of infinite number of blessed qualities.
(g) God is our Father, Mother, Friend, Lover, Beloved, Support, Innermost Reality, Life of our life, and what not.

q: Why do we respect God so much?
a: (a) (i) We respect anyone for his/her merits or superior qualities. But all the possible merits and superior qualities in all respects are in God to an infinite degree.

(ii) We respect parents and other elders as they are ‘older’ in this world and are supposed to be wiser and know more about the world and about human life than us. But God is the ‘Oldest’ -- pre-existing before the world itself. God is the wisest and knows ‘everything’ about the world and about ‘life’.

(iii) Parents are also respected because they are like ‘causes’ and we are ‘effects’. But God is the ‘Ultimate Cause’ and everything and everybody is an ‘effect’ coming out of God. That is why we respect God ‘so much’, though it is much less than as much we should respect God.

(b) God is also the source of any good merit found anywhere. Hence when we respect anyone we are respecting God reflected in that person. If we know this, we will love and respect God with all our heart and soul.

q: Where is the existence of God?
a: (a) God exists everywhere, permeates every atom; is also beyond everything in his own nature.
(b) God is ever present -- hiding -- in the heart-cave of every living being.

q: If there is a God, why don’t we see Him?
a: (i) Because God is the innermost Reality of everything while we are normally constituted seeing things from outside and require very special training to be able to see the inside.

(ii) One great sage always used to say that God is the abiding reality in all of us. So, sometimes people asked him, "You say that God is the abiding reality, then why don’t we see Him?" He used to reply spontaneously repeating the same question in a different tone. He used to say -- "What a pity! Though God is the abiding reality, why don’t we see Him?" The ‘meaning’ of this reply is that the question should be asked neither as a challenge nor as doubt but as yearning and pathos! Let us see a historical incident –

(iii) Narendranath Dutta was born on 12th January 1863. During his college days "Professor William Hastie, the noted scholar", was "his Principal at the General Assembly’s Institution. One day during the absence of the professor of English he took over the literature class. He was explaining Wordsworth’s ‘Excursion’, where the state of trance is referred to, ... But the students did not understand what he meant by trance. Professor Hastie then said, ‘Such an experience is the result of purity of mind and concentration on some particular object, and it is rare indeed, particularly in these days. I have seen only one person who has experienced that blessed state of mind, and he is Ramakrishna Paramahamsa of Dakshineshwar. You can understand if you go there and see for yourself.’ It was thus that Narendra first heard of his future Master." ... (Life

of Sw.V. Vol.I P.47-48). In the meanwhile, "Narendranath believed in a formless God ..., but ... he was convinced that if God really existed He would surely appear in answer to the sincere prayers of the devotees. He felt that there must be a way of realizing him, else life would be futile”. "In his longing to know the Truth Narendranath turned to Maharshi Devendranath Tagore, who was ... living in retirement (seclusion) in a boat on the Ganges ... Narendranath, tense with excitement, flung out the question: ‘Sir, have you seen God?’ The Maharshi was unable to answer and contented himself with: ‘My boy, you have the yogi’s eyes’. Narendranath came away disappointed. He went to the leaders of other religious sects, and not one of them could say that he had seen God. Where then should he go?"

"He then remembered Sri Ramakrishna, ... Ramachandra Dutta ... said to him, ‘If you have a real desire to realize God, then come to the Master (Sri Ramakrishna) at Dakshineshwar’. ... Around this time, Surendranath Mitra, who was a neighbor, also invited him to accompany him to Dakshineshwar in his horse-drawn carriage. Narendranath accepted the invitation and in the company of two of his friends went for the first time to Dakshineshwar one day in December of 1981." (Life of Sw.V. Vol. I P.59-61)

"Sri Ramakrishna represented ... the India of the Upanishads. To him came Naren with all the doubts and skepticism of the modern age, unwilling to accept even the highest truths of religion without verification, yet with a zeal for Truth burning within him." (P.5) Swami Vivekananda recounts: "I sat and watched him ... I crept near him and asked him the question which I had asked so often: ‘Have you seen God, Sir.’ ‘Yes, I see Him just as I see you here, only in a much more intense sense. God can be realized, one can see and talk to Him as I am seeing and talking to you. But who cares? People shed torrents of tears for their wife and children, for wealth or property, but who does so for the sake of God? If one weeps sincerely for Him, He surely manifests Himself.’ That impressed me at once ... I found a man who dared to say that he had seen God, that religion was a reality to be felt, to be sensed in an infinitely more intense way than we can sense the world."(P.77)
Let us try to understand this question and answer.

If an objective type of question is asked in a written examination -- "Have you seen God?" The answer could have been just "Yes, I have seen"; but it is not so in life. There is the life of the questioner, his mind-set and his condition at that point and all this flashes before the clear vision of the sage who has not only seen God but sees human mind through and through. On this background we have already seen that in the pure rational manly mind-set of Narendranath ‘Life’ was blind, futile and unbearable in the absence of a direct intimate knowledge of God the Origin and Director of the world-phenomena -- ‘unbearable’ not in a negative sense, but in the most dynamic sense that ‘there must be a way of realizing him’. He had absolutely focused his faculties of rational understanding and concentrated meditation to achieve that end but had not succeeded so far and hence a type of skepticism was trying to enter his mind -- skepticism never about the ‘existence’ of God but only about the possibility of ‘knowing him directly’ (without which blind vegetating life was ‘meaningless’ to him.) What he was seeking through this question was ‘just one testimony’ of ‘seeing God’ which could drive out the attack of skepticism and enable him to pursue his effort with full vigor, for, as he -- the Swami Vivekananda -- would say with full logical force in future -- "If one man has realized God, every man can do so, because he is also a man."

This was the mind of the questioner which was clear as a crystal to Bhagavan Sri Ramakrishna. Hence we see that the first thing to be noted about the answer is its spontaneity, certainty, clarity -- "Yes" said he -- which would at once put Narendranath’s troubled mind to rest, drive away the possibility of skepticism and put him on the positive course. The next thing we

notice is the present (factual or habitual) tense of "I see him" in place of superficially expected "I have seen". To see God requires penetrative vision and if you have achieved it, it is always yours. What is the fun if you see God once and become the same superficial person again? God has to become a permanent factor of awareness. But still lot more remains to be said. Narendra who knew all about direct perception, hallucination, imagination, hypothesis etc. might have again got a doubt about that God-vision -- hence Sri Ramakrishna added -- "just as I see you". It removes the mixture of ‘imagination’ etc. no doubt. But even this was not enough. Sri Ramakrishna knew that the philosophical aspect of modern science would tell us sooner or later that all that we call direct perception is itself ‘image catching’. Whenever we feel that we are seeing a chair outside, we are actually reacting to the vibration caused in the optical nerves by the image formed on the retina due to (supposed) rays from the thing outside falling on it. Hence on analysis we find that there is so much mediacy in our perceptions that they lose their directness. God has to be perceived "in a much more intense sense", and that is what Sri Ramakrishna adds as a matter of truth and also as a point to be answered in Narendra’s mind! And then he continues by way of emphasizing the reality of this vivid directness, -- "God can be realized, one can see and talk to Him as I am seeing and talking to you." And then the necessary condition -- one pointed, all comprehensive yearning -- is described in the remaining part of the answer. And if that emphatic guarantee in the answer assured Narendranath and set him on the course towards the same realization, it can do the same thing to us.
That is why Mahatma Gandhi says -

"The story of Ramakrishna Paramahamsa’s life is a story of religion in practice. His life enables us to see God face to face. ... In this age of skepticism Ramakrishna presents an example of a bright and living faith which gives solace to thousands of men and women who would have otherwise remained without spiritual light."

(iv) Having said all this by way of comprehensive reply to skepticism and doubt, let us now try to objectively answer the question (No.23) asked -- "If there is God, why don’t we see him." The Answer is (i) Because God is hidden inside everything and we only know how to see a thing from the outside (ii) We do not have the needed all comprehensive yearning, (iii) because we have not followed any of the various prescribed methods to do so and (iv) we lack the purity which is absolutely necessary to develop the penetrative vision to see God. "Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God" -- says Jesus Christ.

q: Is it true that God lives in Param Dham (above the sky)?
a: Let us try to understand what Param Dham is and also what is meant by ‘above the sky’.

(a) When we say ‘above’, the crudeness of our thinking makes it appear as if it is something on a great physical hight. Removing this crude idea that in ‘above’ two ideas are mixed up -- (i)’Beyond’ and (ii) Superior -- but both of them may really mean -- ‘inside’. (b) Some people say that God is beyond the 9th ‘cloud’. These ‘clouds’ are the layers of ignorance in our own heart. So beyond all of them means absolutely ‘inside’. (c) Dham means place or location and Param means Supreme, most superior etc. So God lives in Param Dham means God lives in the deepest recesses of human heart -- untouched by all good and bad in the externalized mind of man. Hence Saint Kabir sings: "Lift the layers of the veil to see the most beloved." (d) Let us try to understand in another way. Whenever we see objects outside -- they are located in ‘space’ outside. But when we ‘see’ mental objects like Anger, Hatred, Love, and Peace they are located in the space of the mind. But when we directly perceive God who is the very source of all perception -- being the source of our consciousness and who is of the very nature of consciousness, that undivided
consciousness itself is the location to see God and hence it is called the supreme sky or supreme space or supreme location.

q: Has anyone seen God in the form of Krishna, Rama, Shiva or it is just the image formed in the mind of people and they are following it blindly?
a: (a) Even today there are many people, I know, who see God in the form of Krishna or Rama or Shiva or ... Ramakrishna, sometimes even without their seeking to see God in that form. Let us first see some pages of recent history -
(i) Sri Ramakrishna (1836-1886 AD) narrates --

"Some time passed that way. Ramawat ‘fathers’ (Babajis) -- men of fervent renunciation, devout and dispassionate ... -- began to pour in. ... It was from one of them that ‘Ramlala’ [A metal image depicting child Rama] came to me. ... That ‘father’ served the image for a long time. He took it with him wherever he went. He cooked whatever he got by Bhiksha and offered the cooked food to it. That was not all; he actually saw that Ramlala ate or wished to eat something or wanted to go for a walk or insisted on the satisfaction of a fancy, and so on. ... I also saw Ramlala doing all that. ... As days passed on, Ramlala’s love for me went on increasing. ... I actually saw -- just as I see you before me -- that Ramlala accompanied me. ... On some days the holy ‘father’ would cook food and offer it to Ramlala but could not find him. ... He would then run up here (to Sri Ramakrishna’s room) and find him playing in the room. ... he used to drag Ramlala to his place and feed him. ... The ‘father’ then came one day and said, ‘Ramlala ... has quenched the thirst of my life. My mind is now free from sorrow and pain. ... He lives happily with you and plays and sports; I am now in such a state that I feel happy at his happiness. Therefore, I can now leave him with you and go elsewhere. ...’ saying so and giving Ramlala to me he bade goodbye. Ramlala has been here since then." (Sri Ramakrishna The Great Master, P 526-531) Here everything is objectively real and much more real than the things of the world!

(ii) "The garden-house of Yadunath Mallick is situated to the south of the Kali temple at Dakshineshwar; the Master (Sri Ramakrishna) used to go there now and then for a walk. ... The officers would open the door of the parlor and ask him to sit and rest there for some time. There were some good pictures hanging on the walls of that room. One of those pictures was that of the child Jesus in his mother’s lap. The Master used to say that he sat one day in that parlor and was looking at the picture ... when he felt that the picture came to life. ... The Master came back to Dakshineshwar temple. ... At last, when the third day was about to close, The Master saw, while walking under the Panchvati, that a marvelous god-man of very fair complexion was coming towards him, looking steadfastly at him. As soon as the Master saw that person, he knew that he was a foreigner. He saw that his long eyes had produced a wonderful beauty in his face, and the tip of his nose, though a little flat, did not at all impair that beauty ... and from the bottom of the Master’s pure heart came out with a ringing sound, the words, ‘Jesus!’ ... When we were visiting the Master long after this event, one day he raised the topic of Jesus and said, ‘Well, boys, you have read the Bible; can you tell me what is written in it about the physical features of Jesus? How did he look? We said, ‘Sir, We have not seen this mentioned anywhere in the Bible; but as he was born a Jew, he must have been very fair in complexion, with long eyes and an aquiline nose to be sure.’... The Master said, ‘But I saw that the tip of his nose was a little flat; I don’t know why I saw him like that.’ (Because that is not what we see in the available paintings.) ... We thought, ‘How could be the form seen by him in ecstasy tally with the actual form of Jesus?’. But we came to know, shortly after the Master passed away, that there were ... descriptions of Jesus’s physical features; according to one of them the tip of his nose was a little flat.’ (G.M. P.295-296). (So when the actual person is seen, the photos etc. are left behind.)

(iii) Sri Ramakrishna told Narendranath "... over and over again, ‘God always hears the plaintive prayer of man and he can be seen, heard and touched palpably, being more real than the fact of this conversation of ours. I stake my credit on this.’ On another occasion he said to him, ‘If you cannot accept the form of God or the common well known ideas about Him because they are the products of human thought, but at the same time have faith in the existence of a God, the controller of the universe, He will certainly bestow His grace on you if you offer such a plaintive prayer as this, "O God, I don’t know Thy nature; please manifest Thyself to me as Thou really art".’ ... (Basing upon these instructions) Narendra adopted a new method of practicing meditation from that time on. We have already said that in our meditation on the Lord, with or without forms, we can but think of Him anthropomorphically (i.e. through modes of the human mind). ... Coming to this conclusion ... he prayed to the effect; ‘O God, make me fit to see your real nature.’ He then removed all kinds of thought from his mind and keeping it still and motionless like the flame of a lamp in a windless place, tried to remain in that state. ... Narendra described -- ‘There flowed in my mind a current of serene bliss when I kept it still, devoid of all objects. I felt for a long time even after the end of the meditation, a sort of intoxication under its impulse. ... One day, when I was sitting in that condition at the end of the meditation, I saw the extraordinary figure of a monk appear suddenly, from where I did not know, and stand before me at a little distance filling the room with a divine effulgence ... as if he wanted to say something. ... That face has been indelibly imprinted in my heart. ... Very often it comes to mind that I had the good fortune of seeing Lord Buddha that day’." (Great Master P.797-798) [When God incarnated himself as the Buddha, he had practiced same type of meditation, and that is why, perhaps, he wanted to share some of his experience with Swami Vivekananda!]

(iv) "... Oblivious of surroundings, the Master (Sri Ramakrishna) one day was pacing up and down the verandah extending east to west, to the north-east of his room in the complex of the temple where he was serving as a Pujari, Mathur (who was almost the proprietor of that temple -- a worldly man, skeptical and yet a devotee) was then sitting by himself in one of the rooms of the separate house. ... The place where the Master was pacing was within an easy range of vision from where Mathur was sitting. ... But the event turned out to be something unthinkable and incomprehensible, for Mathur himself ran up in a great flurry to the Master and started weeping. ... Afterwards ... he said, ‘Father, you were walking, and I saw distinctly that it was not you but my Mother in the temple (the Goddess Kali) over there as you were coming forward in this direction and that it was Mahadeva (God Shiva) Himself immediately when you turned about. I thought at first that it was an optical illusion; I rubbed my eyes well and looked, but saw the same thing. This happened as often as I looked.’"(Great Master P. 433)

(v) "On 24 September 1926 Swami Shivananda (A disciple of Sri Ramakrishna) inaugurated the building of the new ashrama in Ootacamund. Later he recited this incident: ‘One year I visited the Nilgiri Hills. Learning that I was there, a Muslim doctor and his family came all the way from Bombay to see me. ... He had been educated in England and had a very good practice. He was accompanied by his wife. ... The doctor said to me, "... my wife is particularly eager to speak to you." ... His wife saluted me with great devotion, and disclosed many intimate things relating to her spiritual life. ... She worships the child Krishna and occasionally has visions of him. ... It is her conviction that her chosen deity, Krishna, has been born as Ramakrishna.’(God Lived with them, P.165)
(b) These incidents should suffice, and hence, for my own reasons, I do not wish to put in writing the incidents connected with people known to me.

q: How should we recognize God?
If there is any chaotic condition in the world, it is said that an incarnation (avatar) is sent to the earth. If such a thing happens in this age, how will we recognize it?
a: Please refer to the Answer to Q. No. 20 in which we have tried to see what is ‘God’ or what are the distinctive features of God. Now let us see what ‘we’ are apart from our potential divinity. When the consciousness of God reflects on a particular body-mind set up it generates a feeling of ‘I’ in relation to that body-mind. That is what ‘we’ are today -- a reflection of consciousness as if identified with a particular body-mind set up. Now if this body-mind set up itself is ‘I’ and every other thing is ‘not I’ but ‘you’, then the very natural reactions are ‘ego’, ‘narrowness’, ‘attachment’ to those connected with our body and mind, ‘selfishness’, tendency to ‘enjoy’ objects and enjoy relationships etc. But in actual life we see some other things also like non-ego or respect for others, broadness of mind, non-attachment to particulars and a feeling of universal love, unselfishness and doing good to others, a disliking for enjoyment and a liking for tyaga and tapasya, etc. Where from do these things come? From God, no doubt, for such is the nature of God -- the Absolute Perfection -- the repository of infinite blessed qualities etc. And hence whenever and wherever we see the play of these divine qualities to any extent, we should recognize the presence of God. And if we see in any person all these qualities in abundance then we should recognize him/her as a Vibhuti, i.e. very special manifestation of God. And if we see these qualities in full, then we can recognize that person himself/herself as God -- this is the theory of divine incarnations ( avatar ) like Sri Rama, Sri Krishna, Buddha, Jesus and Sri Ramakrishna in our own times.

It is God who comes down in the form of these incarnations so that man may be able to recognize God and also feel sure that God can manifest fully in a human body-mind, and so man himself/herself should struggle intensely to manifest his/her potential Divinity fully in life.

q: How did people get the idea of praying to the Idols?
Is it correct to worship idols?
Should we believe in idol-worship?
a: Some funny confusion seems to have engulfed the Indians due to modern education, grossness of the mind, and ignorance of the ways of mind.
(a) Let us see what Swami Vivekananda has to say.

(i) It was in Rajasthan that Thakur Mangal Singhji, the Maharaja of Alwar, who had become much anglicized, asked, "Well, Swamiji Maharaj, I have no faith in idol worship. What is going to be my fate?" He smiled as he spoke ..."You see, I really cannot worship wood, earth, stone or metal like other people. Does this mean that I shall fare worse in the life hereafter?" The Swami answered, "Well, I suppose every man should follow the religious ideal according to his own faith."... his eyes lighted on a picture of the Maharaja which was hanging on the wall. The Swami commanded the Dewan: "spit on it" ... The Dewan cried out, "What, Swamiji! What are you asking me to do? This is the likeness of our Maharaja! How can I do such a thing?" ... Turning to the Maharaja the Swami continued, "See, your Highness; though this is not you in one sense, in another sense it is you. That was why your devoted servants were so perplexed when I asked them to spit on it. It is a shadow of you; it brings you into their minds. One glance at it makes them see you in it; therefore they look at it with as much respect as they would have in looking at your own person. Thus it is also with the devotees who worship stone and metal images of gods and goddesses. It is because an image brings to their minds their Ishta (that particular aspect of God which is most suitable for that individual), or some special forms and attributes of the Divinity,
and helps them to concentrate, that the devotees worship God in an image. They do not worship the stone or the metal as such.

"I have travelled in many places, but nowhere have I found a single Hindu worshipping an image, saying, ‘O Stone, I worship Thee. O Metal, be merciful to me.’ Everyone, Maharaja, is worshipping the same one God who is the Supreme Spirit, the Soul of Pure Knowledge. And God appears to all according to their understanding and their representation of Him. Prince, I speak for myself. Of course, I cannot speak for you."

Mangal Singhji, who had been listening attentively all this time, said, with folded hands, "Swamiji, I must admit that, looking at image worship in the light you have thrown on it, I have never met anyone who worshipped stone, or wood, or metal. Before this I did not understand its meaning. You have opened my eyes. ..." (Life of SW.V. Vol.I P.268-270)

(ii) And see what happened in Jaipur. Sardar Hari Singh, the Commander-In-Chief of the state ... did not believe in the value of images, and even after hours of discussion with the Swami remained unconvinced. In the evening they went out for a walk. As they were going along the footpath they came upon some devotees carrying the image of Sri Krishna and singing devotional songs as they went. The Swami and the Sardar watched the procession for a while. Suddenly the Swami touched Hari Singh and said, "Look there, see the living God!" The eyes of the sardar fell on the image of Lord Krishna, and he stood there transfixed, with tears of ecstasy trickling down his cheeks. When he returned to ordinary consciousness, he exclaimed, "Well, Swamiji, that was a revelation to me. What I could not understand after hours of discussion, was easily comprehended through your touch. Truly, I saw the Lord in the image of Krishna!" (ibid P. 278)

(b) And hence says Swami Vivekananda -- (i) All men are born idolaters. The lowest man is an animal. The highest man is perfect. And between these two, all have to think in sound and color, in doctrine and ritual. The test of having ceased to be an idolater is: when you say ‘I’, doe s the body come into your thought or not? If it does, then you are still a worshipper of idols. (C.W.of Sw.V.Vol.8, P.229-230)

(ii) The man who is bowing down before the idol; ... It is peculiar to the Hindus. The man is before the idol, and he shuts his eyes and tries to think, "I am He; I have neither life nor death; I have neither father nor mother; I am not bound by time or space; I am Existence infinite, Bliss infinite and Knowledge infinite; I am He, I am He." ... this he repeats and then says, "O Lord, I cannot conceive Thee in myself; I am a poor man.”... You may take the most learned man you have and ask him to think of spirit as spirit; he cannot ... It is impossible to think of spirit without training. (Vol.8,P 210-211)

(iii) Among the Jews, idol worship is condemned, but they had a temple in which was kept a chest which they called an ark, in which the Tables of the Law were preserved, and above the chest were two figures of angels with wings outstretched, between which the Divine Presence was supposed to manifest itself as a cloud. That temple has long since been destroyed, but the new temples are made exactly after the old fashion, and in the chest religious books are kept. The Roman Catholics and the Greek Christians have idol-worship in certain forms. The image of Jesus and that of his mother are worshipped. Among Protestants there is no idol-worship, yet they worship God in a personal form, which may be called idol-worship in another form. Among Parsees and Iranians fire-worship is carried on to a great extent. Among Mohammedans the prophets and great and noble persons are worshipped, and they turn their faces towards the Kaaba when they pray. These things show that men at the first stage of religious development have to make use of something external, and when the inner self becomes purified they turn to more abstract conceptions. "When the Jiva is sought to be united with Brahman it is best, when meditation is practiced it is mediocre, repetition of names is the lowest form, and external worship is the lowest of the low." But it should be distinctly understood that even in practicing the last there is no sin. Everybody ought to do what he is able to do; and if he be dissuaded from that, he

will do it in some other way in order to attain his end. So we should not speak ill of a man who worships idols. He is in that stage of growth, and, therefore, must have them; wise men should try to help forward such men and get them to do better. But there is no use in quarrelling about these various sorts of worship. (Vol.3, P.362-363)

(iv) It has become a trite saying that idolatry is wrong, and every man swallows it at the present time without questioning. I once thought so, and to pay the penalty of that I had to learn my lesson sitting at the feet of a man who realized everything through idols; I allude to Ramakrishna Paramahansa. If such Ramakrishna Paramahansas are produced by idol worship, what will you have -- the reformer’s creed or any number of idols? I want an answer. Take a thousand idols more if you can produce Ramakrishna Paramahansas through idol-worship, and may God speed you! Produce such noble natures by any means you can. Yet idolatry is condemned! Why? Nobody knows. Because some hundreds of years ago some man of Jewish blood happened to condemn it? That is, he happened to condemn everybody else’s idols except his own. If God is represented in any beautiful form or any symbolic form, said the Jew, it is awfully bad; it is sin. But if He is represented in the form of a chest, with two angels sitting on each side, and a cloud hanging over it, it is the holiest of the holy. If God comes in the form of a dove, it is holy. But if He comes in the form of a cow, it is heathen superstition; condemn it! That is how the world goes. That is why the poet says, "what fools we mortals be!" (Vol.3,P.218)
(c) And what then is Sri Ramakrishna’s final advice? --

1. While raising a building, the scaffolding is indispensable; but when the work is completed, no one feels the necessity of it. So also image-worship is necessary in the beginning but not afterwards.

2. A marksman learns to shoot by first having big objects to shoot at; and as he acquires more and more facility in shooting, he aims more and more easily at the smaller marks on the target. So when the mind has been trained to focus on images having forms, it is easy for it do so on things having no form.
3. As a toy fruit or a toy elephant reminds one of the real fruit and the living animal, so do the images that are worshipped remind one of God who is formless and eternal.

4. You were talking of images made of clay. There arises a necessity for them too. These various forms used for worship have been provided to suit the needs of different men at different stages of spiritual evolution.
5. Why call it an earthen image? The Divine image is made of spirit (consciousness).

6. Why do these images rouse the idea of mud and clay, stone and straw, in your mind? Why can you not realize the presence of the eternal, blissful, all-conscious Mother (The Supreme Reality) even in these forms?

7. If a worshipper is convinced that the images of the Deity in the shape of various gods and goddesses are verily divine, he reaches God through their worship. But if he holds them to be nothing better than mud and straw and clay, to him the worship of such images does no good.

8. If there is anything wrong in image-worship, does He not know that all worship is meant for Him? He will surely be pleased to accept that worship, knowing that it is meant for Him alone. Love God; that is the duty nearest to you.

9. When one sees God, one realizes that everything, images and all, is a manifestation of the Spirit. To him the image is not made of clay but of spirit (consciousness). (Sayings of Sri Ramakrishna,P.100-101)
Now we are in a position to find answers to all questions on idol worship by ourselves.

q: Are the stories about God true?
a: The ‘stories’ of God can be divided into several categories.

(a) Biographical and historical (b) Legendary and mythological (c) Allegorical (d) mixed. In our country (i) Valmiki Ramayana and the original Mahabharata which was named as ‘Jaya’ granth by its author Vyasa belong to the first category and are called itihasa , i.e., iti-ha-aasa -- meaning ‘like this-it is well known that-it happened.’ While the stories contained in all the Puranas come mostly under (b) (c) and (d). The purpose of the writers of these Puranas is not to give information about facts of biography or history but, in the words of Swami Vivekananda -- "Philosophy of course is the essence of every religion; mythology explains and illustrates it by means of the more or less legendary lives of great men, stories and fables of wonderful things, and so on; rituals give to that philosophy a still more concretized form, so that everyone may grasp it -- ritual is in fact concretized philosophy." (C.W.Vol.1,P.72) "Some historical truth is the nucleus of every Purana. The object of the Puranas is to teach mankind the sublime truth in various forms; and even if they do not contain any historical truth, they form a great authority for us in respect of the highest truth which they inculcate. ... Hinduism stands independent of any man, and for the purpose of estimating the philosophical truth contained in any Purana, we need not consider the question whether the personages treated of therein were really material men or fictitious characters. The object of the Puranas was the education of mankind, and the sages who constructed them contrived to find some historical personages and to superimpose upon them all the best or worst qualities just as they wanted to, and laid down the rules of morals for the conduct of mankind." (C.W.Vol.5 P.207-208)

q: Are our prayers and meditations really heard by God?
a: A Christian saint, Brother Lawrence, says -- "When we talk and God listens, it is called prayer; and when God talks (i.e. we get responses from God within) and we listen (our mind becomes absolutely fixed), then it is meditation."

q: If we pray to God for something do we really get it?
a: Ours is to pray, to give or not is God’s discretion.

q: Is it necessary to offer Prasad to God? How does He accept it?
a: Let us correct our language a little. When we ‘offer’ anything to God, it should be called Naivedya. (Naivedya = offering); it becomes prasad (sanctified food) only after God has accepted it.

(a) God has created the world; God has created everything in the world; God has created us; God has created our capacity to do anything; God has created food; God has created the capacity in us to eat food. Everything is God’s. Everything belongs to God. If we understand this thoroughly, should we not think and feel every time that we owe to God our eating food or enjoying the world or doing things? If we do not, we will be thieves, and our eating etc. will be sinful and we shall be sinful -- says the Bhagavad Gita.(3, 12-13)
(b) If we love anyone really -- do we not feel much happier by feeding him/her first and then eating the residual? If we do not feel that way, aren’t we too selfish and love our
enjoyments more than anything else? Those who ‘love’ God feel that way. And hence they offer everything to God or rather they try to make God eat first before they do so.

(c) Similarly, if you have high regard for someone do you not feel like serving him/her? Those who have highest regard for God feel like this. Offering food and other items becomes a part of those acts of service. All these actions help us to feel the living presence of God.
(d) How does God accept the food offered? Let us read some narration from ‘Sri Ramakrishna The Great Master’ (P.146-147)

“Formerly when he (Sri Ramakrishna) offered cooked food etc., to the Mother (Goddess Kali) he used to see an extraordinary ray of light coming out beaming from Her eyes, touching all the offered articles, taking their essential parts and withdrawing itself again into Her eyes. Now he saw that even before the offering was made, the same Mother sat down to take the offerings in Her very Person, illumining the temple with the effulgence of Her holy person. One day Hriday (Sri Ramakrishna’s nephew) came suddenly at the time of the worship and saw that the Master (Sri Ramakrishna) had taken in his hands an Arghya consisting of China roses and Bilva Leaves, which he was going to offer to the lotus feet of the divine Mother. He was absorbed thinking of Her, when he cried out suddenly, saying, "Wait, wait. Let me utter the Mantra first, and then Thou mayest take it." He then offered the food ritually before finishing the worship.
(e) There is an independent corroboration with some more explanation in a passage from the "The Gospel of the Holy Mother"(P.101-102) --
Disciple: Does the Master really partake of the food that you offer him? Mother (Holy Mother Sri Sarada Devi): Yes, He does.
Disciple: But we do not see any sign of it.

Mother: A light comes out of his eyes and licks all the articles of food. His ambrosial touch replenishes them again. So there is no decrease. ... Why? Does the Master require any food? He doesn’t. He eats the food offering only for the gratification of the devotees. The sacred prasad purifies the heart. The mind becomes impure, if one eats food without first offering to God.
Disciple: Does the Master really partake of the food offering?
Mother: Yes, do I not notice whether he partakes of the food or not? The Master takes his seat before the plate and then partakes of the food.
Disciple: Do you then actually see it?

Mother: Yes, In the case of some offerings, he actually eats and in other cases he merely looks at them. Take your own case. You don’t like to eat all things at all times. Nor do you relish the food offered by anyone and everyone. It is like that.

q: What is spiritual strength?
a: When we are climbing steps, we have to leave our hold on the lower step before we can put our foot on the next higher step. But a tendency of not leaving the previous step is present in our mind and it obstructs us. In such a situation, we require the courage to go ahead, the conviction of ultimate success and the strength of leaving the previous step. This is called spiritual strength. There is a proverb in Hindi "KUCH PAANE KE LIYE KUCH KHONA PADATA HAI!" -- i.e., to get something worthwhile we have to lose some trash -- But we ask sometimes -- KYA KUCH KHOYE BINA PAA NAHI SAKTE -- ‘Can we not get what we want without losing even the trash?’ This is spiritual weakness.

q: What is the effect of Mantra (especially Gayatri Mantra) on our body and mind?
a: (a) Let us start with the meaning of Gayatri -- part by part.
Aum = God, the Absolute, Ultimate Reality.
[Bhuh = Earth; Bhuwah = Intermediate space; Svah = Skies]
Bhurbhuvah Svah = The Absolute Reality pervades the earth, intermediate space and the skies.
[Tat = It, Savituh = of the Sun]
Tat Savituh = It is like the luminousity of the Sun OR Sun is the symbol of its self-luminosity.
But the sun is the source of physical light while the Reality is the source of awareness and knowledge.
Varenyam = Adorable -- because it is supremely wise.
Bhargo Devasya = The shine of the Self-luminous [as explained above]
Dheemahi = We meditate on It (as the Absolute and pervading Reality and as the source of awareness and knowledge).
Dhiyoyo = Intellects
Nah = ours
Prachodayat = May God, the source of our knowledge, kindle, awaken our intellectual faculty.
(b) In the Indian tradition this mantra was taught by the father to his son/daughter in presence of the teacher who was to take him/her for being educated under his guidance.
(c) If repeated in morning, mid-noon and evening, its effects are
(i) Freshness, vigor and poise of mind and intellect are maintained.
(ii) The feeling that God is my own innermost reality and source of my intelligence and power gives a hold on God, devotion, strength and confidence.
(iii) The repetition of Gayatri or any such mantra representing God increases the power of concentration and memory.
(iv) It checks the mind from becoming wayward.
(vi) It generates spiritual eminence.

q: What are the benefits of meditation?
a: (a) Let us take an allegory to understand, first, as to what is ‘meditation’. During the British regime the administration used to appoint sergeants for night patrolling on the streets of big cities. These sergeants used to carry a lantern each which was shaded on their side. So, in the light of the lantern the sergeant could see all people and all that was happening, and also all people could see each other but could not see the sergeant.

Let us think of such a situation, now. What could be the different responses of the people involved in it? Most of the people would neither bother to look at the light nor bother about the sergeant but remain satisfied in going about their own pursuits. A few people would feel that they could not have gone about their business without the light, and they would say "Thank you, O light!" and a fewer still would say "Thank you, O sergeant!" without even looking in that

direction. Some rare people now and then would look at the light and bow down in that direction. Now, light cannot stand or move by itself, hence there has to be somebody holding it, and the fact that we are not seeing that person implies that there is shade on that side. This is the inference. It is also known from the newspapers that there is a sergeant holding the light -- seeing the people and helping them. So, some one -- different from others -- would be keen to ‘know’ and ‘see’ and ‘talk to’ the sergeant. Hence looking in that direction he would pray, "Sergeant, Sir, will you please turn the light towards your face, so that I can see you? And will you please talk to me!" The sergeant would oblige him if he felt the sincerity in the prayer.

Now, it is the light of God -- who is Existence-Consciousness-Bliss -- which reflects in our minds and in the world enabling us to have this interaction. One feels respectful grateful love called Bhakti for the Source of everything and prays and tries for turning the direction of the light reflected in our soul towards its source. This in short is the philosophical foundation of meditation.
(b) But, there are almost infinite variations in human temperaments, and hence the actual practice of meditation takes innumerable forms. Let us discuss a few broad categories:

(i) Karma Yogi’s meditation : The predominantly active mind -- in the early morning, before he/she has plunged into the activities of the day, sits quietly and tries to feel deeply in his/her heart that God is present there as the source of consciousness and intelligence and all the powers for work being manifested in him/her and he/she is God’s beloved servant who loves his/her Master very dearly and wishes to carry out God’s will, or he/she is merely the instrument through which God is going to get His work done etc.
Throughout the day whenever units of work are complete, he/she tries to be with God the master for just a few seconds before the next work starts.

In the evening or at bed time he/she tries to introspect, and becoming aware of his/her follies of ego, selfishness, haughtiness etc., prays to God in the depth of the heart and surrenders all the actions good and bad and their fruits to God and seeks God’s help to do better next day.

(ii) Bhakti Yogi’s meditation : The loving mind loves his/her God both inside the depths of the heart and outside through some image, photo, symbol, book etc. which are kept in secluded place, keeps that place clean, decorates it with flowers, burns incense, waves a light and reads a devotional text -- tries to feel God as the very dearest center of his life, steadily visualizes the chosen form of God on a lotus in the heart, concentrates there lovingly and repeats a mantra for as long as he/she can. Repeats the same thing in the evening -- may be with some other text -- but using the same mantra.

(iii) The Rajayogi’s meditation: The introspective self-observant mind -- is very harsh on himself/herself -- tries to keep the mind absolutely still, observes what is going on in his/her body and mind from surface to depth -- crossing layer after layer and checking the mind from within till he/she comes to have total control of mind -- keep it absolutely still so that the innermost Reality may shine in it in Its true form and thus gets released from all drawbacks etc.

(iv) The Jnana Yogi’s meditation: The mind which is aware that this world including his body-mind etc. is only an appearance on the surface -- the Reality is one without a second -- Undivided Existence-Consciousness-Bliss -- listens raptly to the experiences of the sages recorded in the Upanishads and similar scriptures, reflects this truth on all his/her thinking, feelings and action and always tries to remain deeply absorbed in such awareness.

(c) These are very broad outlines. Because the human mind is usually an overlap of different types and has innumerable varieties -- meditation suitable for each individual is to be learnt from expert guides only.
(d) Now we will be in a position to understand the ‘benefits’ of meditation which can be enumerated as below -
(i) Everything positive in life grows, everything negative recedes.
(ii) There is a flow of supreme inner joy not dependent on anything in the world and hence
(iii) Mind has a positive outlook.
(iv) It is filled with vigor, strength and confidence.
(v) Is active with clarity of vision, but never restless or out of control.
(vi) Is controlled, steady and steadily active.
(vii) Is concentrated and properly focused.
(viii) Physical health is toned up.
(ix) Memory and power of retention increases.
(x) Potential divinity is manifested more and more
(xi) and, ultimately God is realized, the supreme Goal of life is achieved, man/woman himself/herself becomes divine.
(e) Swami Vivekananda says -

"Meditate! The greatest thing is meditation. It is the nearest approach to spiritual life -- the mind meditating. It is the one moment in our daily life that we are not at all material -- the soul thinking of itself, free from all matter -- this marvelous touch of the soul!" (C.W.5, 253)

q: What is Brahma-Muhurta? Why is this time best for meditation or doing puja? Does the effect of Mantra depend on time?
a: (a) Precisely speaking, Brahma Muhurta is little more than three-quarters of an hour preceding sunrise -- e.g. if the Sun rise at a place on a particular day is at 6 a.m., then 5.12 a.m. to 6 a.m. would be the Brahma Muhurta for that place on that day. It is called Brahma Muhurta, which means the period of time when Brahman, the all-pervading Reality is comparatively more manifest in nature and in human mind also.

(b) The nature outside as well as in our body and mind has 3 functional phases which occur cyclically. They are called Sattva, Rajas and Tamas. Sattva is the quality of pure existence and is characterized by equipoise, serenity, balance of mind and a tendency for pure knowledge, devotion, unselfishness etc. Rajas is of the nature of coloring of the mind and is characterized by likes and dislikes, passions, restlessness, de-control etc. Tamas is of the nature of darkness and is characterized by ignorance, dullness, inertia, narrowness, selfishness, delusion, inability to exert or improve oneself etc. All these three are parts of life and occur cyclically. So far as outside nature is concerned, during day, when the sun is warm it is Rajas; when night falls it is Tamas; and Sattva occurs only for a short while in the 4 null points -- (i) when night is over and day has not begun, (ii) when day is over and night has not yet come, (iii) Mid-noon and (iv) exactly mid-night. If human life also takes its natural course then we allow Tamas to have its course in the night, and when that is over, but before we are warmed up, our mental mode is that of Sattva. Then follows Rajas, and so on. It is when the existence is pure i.e. in the mode of Sattva, that it expresses the presence of God. If we catch this period we are likely to succeed more in the thought of God specially in meditation and also in mantra japa or mental worship etc.

q: How do we attain Moksha?
a: Please refer to Answer to Q. 1 & 2 to get an idea of Moksha. Let us again try to understand it in two ways.

1. Suppose (figuratively speaking) God is sitting in a place and to reach Him there he has dropped several ropes which he is continuously pulling towards himself. When we catch one of these ropes and hold fast to it we are pulled by God to himself and we attain Moksha. If we catch several ropes and hold fast we may be quickly pulled. What are these ropes in this figure? Karma yoga, Bhakti yoga, Raja Yoga, Jnana Yoga and all the paths of Sadhana laid down by all the religions and sects of the world are the ropes spread by God himself for different temperaments of human beings.
