And taking them and practicing steadfastly is like holding fast to the ropes.
2. Coming out of the analogy, let us know -- that Moksha is not a place to be reached, but the realization of God, here, in this human life. Moksha means ‘Freedom’. Freedom from what? From bondages.

What are the bondages? -- (i) Our wrong identification with a particular body-mind set up which is changing continuously. (ii) As a result of this wrong identification, we have a feeling of limitedness, incompleteness. This is bondage. (iii) To remove these feelings we try to get something from outside -- but anything added from outside, however big it may be does not change our limitedness or incompleteness. Rather we get lost under those outside accumulations, and that is again a bondage. (iv) For us this body-mind only is ‘I’ and everything else is ‘not I’ or ‘you’. Behind everything is the same God who is hid den but His reflection makes everything appear real, animated and pleasurable. This apparent pleasurableness together with our limitedness give rise to infinite desires which in turn generate other passions -- anger, greed, delusion due to infatuation, intoxication and jealousy/competition and the like. These are all bondages. (v) The desires do not end every time we try to satisfy them; they increase like fire supplied with fuel. So the bondage continues. (vi) The body collapses when exhausted in the pursuit of desires but desires do not stop, hence we are born again and again and this rotation goes on -- called the bondage of Samsara.

In spite of all this we are potentially divine and if that divinity is fully manifested we no longer feel identified with any particular body-mind -- no more feeling of limitedness or incompleteness, no craving for getting something from outside and no more getting lost under any outside thing, no more drags of desires, no more troubles from passions, no more burning of the fire of desires, no more compulsion to go through births and deaths again and again. Then what? Then permanent and Absolute Perfection, Permanent and Absolute Knowledge, Permanent and Absolute Bliss -- everything like that of God -- this is Moksha.
How does one ‘realize’ that -?

By steadfast and intense practice of everything which helps the manifestation of divinity and removal of the identification with a particular body-mind. This practice, according to individual temperaments is called as different yoga’s or different paths of sadhana laid down by different religions.

q: Can a person be a devotee of God without leaving worldly pleasures or will he have to leave his family and turn into a ‘ vairagi’?
a: Please do not mix up separate things -- viz. worldly ‘pleasures’ and ‘Family’ life. There are many people around who lead a family life and yet are very much devoted to God. If you read the book called ‘The Gospel of Sri Ramakrishna’ ( Sri Ramakrishna Vachanamrita in Hindi) you will find that almost from first page to the last Sri Ramakrishna is telling the householders ‘how’ they can be devoted to God.

q: Our parents gave birth to us. How was God born?
God created us, who created God?
From where has God come?
a: These questions which appear rational and rather smart on the surface are found to be irrational and foolish on a little thought. ‘Birth’, ‘coming’, ‘creation’ -- what do they mean? Our conception about every object in this universe and about the universe itself is that there was a time when this was not there, nothing of this was there, and then it came into being. So naturally we ask who created it, from where it came or who gave it birth. We are also clearly assuming the pre-existence of something which could be the 'cause’ of this.

Now, God has been understood as the eternally existing Reality. There was never a time when God was not there. Even when time itself was not there, God was there. So no question of ‘coming’, ‘birth’, ‘creation’ can apply or have any meaning in relation to God. Our experience of the finite cannot be projected to the infinite God -- who pre-exists everything that is born and continues to exist when all is gone. And so we call God as beginningless and endless -- Absolute -
- Existence – one, without a second.

q: What happens after death?

In the ‘Gita’ it is written that when the soul leaves the body, it roams about and then gets into a new body, i.e., soul never dies but it changes body which is mortal. Are all these things true? Please explain.
What kind of life does the soul have after death?
How can we perceive that life from our frame of reference?
Why does a person forget after death the affectionate relationships which we have on this earth? Can they be not kept intact after death?
a: It is not written in the ‘Gita’ that when the soul leaves the body, it roams about and then gets into a new body; but what is written in the Gita as well as the Upanishads can be explained as follows:

(a) If we start from the present life, we see that we have a mind, and a body which is corresponding to the mind at birth. As we live our life, the body evolves and decays mostly according to the fixed potential which it has at birth, while the mind being much more changeable has two forces working on it - (i) the starting potential and (ii) our relatively free will, thoughts and feelings, which are molded by the training which we receive in the world and the tendencies etc. which we consciously cultivate.

(b) Suppose, out of the almost infinite tendencies playing in the human mind, a person has cultivated the cat-like tendencies -- e.g., moving about stealthily etc., -- more than the others, then at the time of death the mind of that person has mostly become a cat-mind. So when this present body collapses, the cat-mind necessarily gets a cat-body -- and so forth.
(c) Hence the following categories (types) of life after death have been described by the scriptures:-

(i) Any life lower than that of a human being -- even a tree or a stone etc. In Upanishads and Gita there is no mention of a separate place called ‘ Narak’, but the species below humans is the lowest life.
(ii) Rebirth as man with human mind with all the special tendencies gathered in this life -- that is why we see different talents and characters in human beings.

[Both these types of births are taken at the very point of death of this body. The ‘Chhandogya Upanishad’ describes the process by the example of a leech travelling from leaf to leaf -- it catches the next leaf and then leaves the hold on the previous leaf.]

(iii) When a person has been doing exceptionally good works and accumulating exceptionally good tendencies, his mind is transformed into a god-mind. For enjoying the happiness resulting in such a mind, a body made of gross material like that of man or animals cannot suffice, and hence he gets a very different type of divine body and goes to live in a different type of abode. This is called ‘ Swarga‘(heaven). There are different categories of these heavens depending upon how much higher the mind has become. Here he/she lives for a very long time as that body does not decay so quickly.

(iv) When a person thinks of God he gets different types of changes whereby he feels nearness of God, tangible presence of God etc. Such a person goes to those spheres where he has a different type of bliss resulting from God-vision. The highest among these is called Vaikuntha by the devotees of Vishnu, Kailash by the devotees of Shiva, Sach-khand by the Sikhs etc. and Satya-loka or Brahmaloka by philosophers.

(v) Those who get full God-realization, identification with God, Absolute perfection and infinitude in human life -- do not have to ‘go’ anywhere. Even in this life they do not feel bound by this body -- they experience the infinitude even while living and hence when the body drops, they continue to permanently experience the identification with God the Infinite.

(vi) Except (v) none others are permanent, and after exhausting the respective momentum of (i) (iii) & (iv) we are again born as human beings to get a chance to struggle for full God-realization. It is important to note that the nearness to God achieved in (iv) is present in the next life also, and therefore the struggle gets a corresponding higher start.
(d) ‘To perceive that life from the present frame of reference’ -- this can be done in three ways:-
(i) To intellectually understand as above with the help of scriptures.
(ii) To read the descriptions in the lives of extraordinary persons like Sri Ramakrishna who perceive all these types of beings and describe them vividly.
(iii) To develop higher and universal consciousness which will enable us to directly perceive all these.
(e) Compared to the almost infinite life of an individual till he/she attains perfection, one single human life is too small a span to make permanent impact of the ‘affectionate attachments’.

q: What is Sin?
a: A very simple and universal answer is given by the great sage Vyasa as in this pithy couplet:
Shruti-smriti-puraneshu vyasasya vachanadwayam;
Paropakarah punyaya papaya parapeedanam.
"Doing good to others is holy action; while giving trouble to others is sin."

q: What is heaven and hell?
It is said that one does bad actions he/she goes to hell (Narak), and if one does good actions, he/she goes to heaven (Swarga). So where is heaven and hell?
a: Though these questions have been replied along with Q.45 to 48, let us have a fresh look at them.

What happens if we do ‘good’ actions? The heart expands. The heart becomes purer. The mind becomes less restless. God or Atman present within as abiding Reality has Bliss as Its own nature. This bliss of God or Atman reflects better in that heart which is not restless, which is broad and pure. This reflection is called the inner happiness. This continues even after the present body is exhausted. The mind which has been purified, expanded and steady is with us even after this body is dropped and so we have our own inner bliss -- this is called going to heaven (Swarga). What happens if we do bad actions? The heart becomes contracted; it becomes impure; the mind becomes restless. The Bliss i.e. Atman gets a distorted reflection in our mind and we feel miserable. This continues even after death -- so we remain miserable even when this body in which we do those bad actions is not there. This is called going to hell (Narek). Jesus Christ calls God as "father in heaven"; he also tells us, "The kingdom of heaven is within you", and again he says -- "Blessed are the pure in heart for they shall see God." Connecting these three utterances, we can understand that the pure heart is called "heaven" in which ‘God’ is ‘experienced’.

q: What are ghosts?
Do ghosts and spirits really exist?
a: There are certain exceptions to the rules of rebirth mentioned in the answers to Q.45-48. When a person is born, he has to exhaust a certain type and amount of stored up momentum, in that life through that body. But if he dies of an unnatural death through accident or suicide etc., without having worked out the momentum meant to be exhausted in that body, he/she does not get a body immediately. He/she has a mind, and desires, but not the body to work them out. Such are ghosts. ‘Spirits’ also may be such ghosts or sometimes a little higher types of beings. These ghosts and spirits do remember affections and associations of the previous life which they might have left incomplete, and sometimes try to help their relations of that previous life or sometimes are hostile to them because of their unfulfilled desires. It has been commonly believed and also has been verified sometimes that they get released from that state if someone knowing them prays for them or makes some devotional offerings to God for their sake.

As far as the truth of their existence is concerned, one should know two things. (i) They do exist because they have been perceived by sages and others having immaculate wider range of perceptions. (ii) And yet, ninety-nine per-cents of the cases reported by ordinary people are subjective imaginations.

q: In the area of religion is there any place of astrology?
How can we interpret the effect of planets in relation to religion?
If the effects of planets are so powerful, what role do we would give to God?
a: Rather than entering into any elaborate discussion on this aspect, I would like to quote the great saint Tulasidas -
## JANAKINATH SAHAY KARE JAB KAUN BIGAR KARE NARA TERO
## SURAJA MANGALA SOMA BHRUGUSUTA BUDHA ARU GURU VARADAYAKA TERO
## RAHU KETU KI NAHI GAMYATA, SANG SANICHAR HOTA UCHERO

which means -- "when God becomes your helper, who can do any harm to you? Sun, Mars, Moon, Venus, Mercury and Jupiter will become bestower of boons to you. Rahu and Ketu cannot reach you and Saturn will be on the ascent to help you."

q: Is previous birth a fact? Do the actions of a previous birth also influence the present life?
Can we know about previous birth?
a: (a) (i) There is no doubt about the existence of previous births without which the ‘ Sanskaras’ present in this life cannot be explained. These ‘ Sanskaras’ represent the momentum acquired in the past lives. Their result determines largely our birth in a particular species and in a particular family, our life span and the share of pleasure and pain to be experienced by us in this life. On the other hand, our experiences, progress and evolution seen in this life are the resultant of this past momentum plus the effort which we put in this life.
(b) There are perhaps three ways of knowing the previous birth:

(i) The Great Sage Patanjali tells us that if we are established in ‘Aparigraha’, we absolutely refuse to accept any free gift from anybody – and are firmly established in this attitude, we shall get the memory of past lives. Swami Vivekananda explains: ‘When a man does not receive presents, he does not become beholden to others, but remains independent and free. His mind becomes pure. With every gift, he is likely to receive the evils of the giver. If he does not receive, the mind is purified, and the first power it gets is memory of past life. (Patanjala Yogasutra 2,39)

(ii) Again in another chapter Patanjali says -- By perceiving the impression, (comes) the knowledge of past life. As explained by Swami Vivekananda -- "Each experience that we have, comes in the form of a wave in the ‘Chitta’, and this subsides and become finer and finer, but is never lost. It remains there in minute form, and if we bring this wave up again, it becomes memory. So if the Yogi can make a Samyama (perfect steady fixed concentration) on these past impressions in the mind, he will begin to remember all his past lives. (3,18)

(iii) In ‘Sri Ramakrishna the Great Master’, Swami Saradanandaji tells of another method for the Jnana Yogi. When the consciousness of non-duality of Reality is cultivated to perfection the mind gets almost God-like purity. And in that mind all the past lives are seen like a cinematographic film.

(iv) Apart from these three methods which depend upon tremendously evolved state of mind, we see in rare cases some people remembering their past lives without any effort. This happens only when the impressions of the past life are too strong. I know the case of a sikh lady born in Chandigarh who remembers her past life as the daughter of a Kashmiri Pundit who used to worship Shiva in the temple of a particular village in Kashmir. Her husband took her to the village mentioned by her and she could easily identify the temple etc.

q: What is the Zeroness (Shunyata) advocated by Indian Philosophers?
a: This has two different phases. One is about the Ultimate Reality and the other is about the transitory world of our experience.

(a) It is only the non-vedic (heterodox) schools which talk of Shunyata (zeroness) regarding the ultimate nature of Reality. The vedic schools never. Reference can be made to Chhandogya Upanishad quoted in answer to Questions 6 to 12. The teacher tells the disciple -- "In the beginning all this was only Absolute Existence – One, without a second. Some people say that in the beginning all this was non-existence alone -- One, without a second. But, my dear one, how can any existence come out of non-existence. Hence, my dear one, all this, in the beginning was Absolute Existence alone – One, without a second." So this is the position regarding the Ultimate Reality.
(b) But reading between the lines, one feels why make a reference at all to what others say? It is done, because, ‘all this’ as we see and feel today -- was surely not there before it was created -
- hence it is necessary to feel the zeroness of the world as it appears to us today, in order to really grasp the ultimate Reality behind and beyond all this.

(c) There is a third context -- the necessity to feel the zeroness or hollowness of ‘ego’ to really get at the Reality behind and beyond. Mahapurushji, a disciple of Sri Ramakrishna used to say -- "If you want the Poorna (the Infinite), you should become Shunya (zero). If ‘you’ become Shunya, you will attain the Poorna (Infinite).

q: How did you come to know about the answers to all these questions we have asked you?
a: (A) Let us start by making a list of the Holy Books I have quoted explicitly or referred to in my own mind while giving these answers.

1. The principal Upanishads -- These are parts of the most ancient Vedic literature. They are 11 in number -- Ishavasya, Katha, Kena, Mundaka, Prasna, Mandukya, Taittiriya, Aitareya, Chhandogya, Brihadaranyaka and the Svetasvatara Upanishads.
2. The Bhagvadgita -- which again is a part of the epic Mahabharata.
3. Sri Ramakrishna the Great Master, by Swami Saradananda
4. The Gospel of Sri Ramakrishna.
5. The Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda.
6. The standard works of other sages, e.g., Sri Shankaracharya, Sri Jnaneswara, Narada etc. and also those of the disciples of Sri Ramakrishna, etc.

It is evident that a lot of my ability to answer questions to the questioner’s satisfaction has come from reading these authoritative books and from trying to understand, assimilate and absorb the thoughts, ideas and ideals expressed therein.
Of course, that is not all.

(B) I lived with a teacher -- a sage -- whose life, behavior, thoughts, knowledge and actions illumined me to a very great extent. Also, either myself or some others in my presence did put these or similar questions to him and received full answers.
(C) Through meditation, unselfish work, devotion to God and contemplation -- more and more knowledge becomes revealed.

q: What is the relation between Education and values?
a: The very purpose of education is inculcation and strengthening of values OR to make life more valuable and worthwhile.

This is clear by the very meaning of the words involved. The new Webster Dictionary explains `education' as "instruction or training by which people learn to develop and use their mental, moral and physical powers" and the same dictionary explains `value' as "the measure of how strongly something is desired for its physical or moral beauty, usefulness, rarity, etc". Paying particular attention to `mental powers' in the definition of education we find the same dictionary stating that `mental' means "of or pertaining to the mind", and `mind' means "the seat of consciousness, thought, feeling and will".

If we combine all these definitions we find that education is that instruction or training by which people learn to develop their powers of thought, feeling and will as well as moral or physical powers, thereby making their life more and more valuable and worthwhile to themselves and to society at large.

q: What is your reading of the present scenario?
a: We are passing through darkest period where education has become totally divorced from its own meaning.

It seems that the we have totally forgotten the purpose of education and as a result we are facing steep decline of moral values, rise and dominance of anti-values like corruption, apathy towards neighbours and nation, etc. etc. and drifting towards chaos.

The present education has totally neglected moral training as well as training of feeling and will, and is only concerned with intellectual gathering of information. Thus we get so-called knowledge without wisdom,-- and man, instead of being transformed from animal to human and human to divine, becomes a learned animal or a skilled criminal. Drastic remedial measures are called for from all concerned, especially from the Government.

q: What is the Government’s responsibility?
a: The Government is primarily responsible for a) Media; b) Syllabus and Course contents in general; c) Syllabus and Course content of Teachers' Training Programmes.
The educators for any person are
(i) Parents, (ii) Educational Institutions, (iii) Society and (iv) Media.
The Media in turn goes on educating the parents and the society.

Hence the Government should see that the media, the course content in Education in general and in the Teachers' Training programmes should be flooded with positive ideas of development of thought, feeling, will, and moral and physical strength.

q: What values are universally accepted and really conducive to man-making?
a: The Supreme values are :-- i) Awareness of potential divinity in oneself resulting in real stable Self-Confidence and healthy positive attitude.
ii) Awareness of potential divinity in others resulting in love and respect for all others irrespective of their caste, creed or nationality.
We can also add :
a. Fearlessness / Boldness b. Purity of Heart c. Constant Pursuit of Higher Values d. Austerity and Struggle for Perfection e. Steadfastness in the pursuit of knowledge.

f. Self-control g. Truthfulness / Uprightness h. Tranquillity / Steadiness / Even-mindedness i. Charity / Nobility / Spirit of sacrifice j. Kindness to Beings k. Humility / Gentleness / Modesty l. Forgiveness / Forbearence / Fortitude m. Cleanliness n. Dignity of manual labour o. Reverence to the teacher p. Introspection q. Non-attachment r. Faith and love for the Almighty God s. Absence of Jealousy, ill-feeling and hatred t. Freedom from Slander u. Absence/Control over Anger v. Non-craving for Enjoyments or Absence of Self-Indulgence w. Absence of Greed x. Absence of Conceit y. Absence of Arrogance and Rudeness.

q: What methods of implementation do you suggest at school, college and University levels?
a: We should orient the entire education system towards it so that education becomes true education.
a) For example, the very appearence and upkeep of the educational institutions and their Surroundings must be thought of as integral parts of `education'.

(i) The campus and buildings in every educational institution have to be kept spotlessly clean and most of the cleaning should be done by the staff and the students supervised by the Principal to inculcate (a) dignity of manual labour, (b) love and regards for that section of the society who keep our city etc. clean, ( c) Cleanliness as a value, and (d) mental and moral benefits derived from cleanliness.
(ii) Great and noble thoughts should be prominently displayed in all possible places.
b) Similarly, we should use all direct and indirect methods of inculcating and strengthening values.
c) At least at school level there should be teacher-parent association -- a forum where values should be discussed and encouraged.
d) At college level groups should be formed under a tutor or counseller to discuss ways and means of imbibing values.

The approach must necessarily be multi-dimensional e) Some of the means suggested are i) compulsory class on moral education at every level ii) the course content, especially of language and literature topics must contain inspiring passages from the lives and teachings of great men of all countries whose lives have been shining examples of values leading to real success and glory of life.
iii) Teachers should be trained for counselling and this must be introduced in all educational institutions for guiding individuals.
iv) Activities like Boy-scouts, N.S.S., etc. should be made a part of education.

q: What should be the basic guidelines of life?
a: 1. Conviction of one’s own and others potential divinity should be the first principle.
2. Faith in oneself, which directly follows from the above conviction.

3. The four cardinal virtues : i. Unselfishness; ii. Deep devotion to God, the Universal Infinite, worshipped in any form or manner; iii. Self-control; iv. Rational understanding of the ultimate nature of things.
4. Devotion to Duty
5. Regularity of spiritual practice.
6. Planned and disciplined life.
7. Zest for knowledge.
8. Following everything that makes oneself strong physically, mentally, morally, spiritually, and avoiding everything which weakens.
9. If one is cent per cent sure about a thing being right, one must have the courage to follow it.

q: Is meditation and long prayers, the only way to reach God?
What should the children do whose first and primary Goal is to study?
a: Let us first think of ‘studies’ and the various motivations etc. involved in it. I was once amidst students of the higher secondary (11th & 12th standard) classes who told me that their parents enjoyed watching T.V. but did not allow them to do so and told them -- "Now you go on studying so that later on you can enjoy these pleasures." They then asked me (I don’t know whether they asked the same question to their parents or not) -- "Why should we not enjoy pleasures now itself? What would happen if we die tomorrow?" I exclaimed -- "Alas! How wrong to motivate towards study by telling that it would give them the route passage (through money?) for the enjoyment of pleasures (which a pig can do best without any education)! Why not tell them that the process of education will help them become well developed individuals by increasing their power of thinking, the capacity of understanding the world and themselves better and better, and by giving them the ability to work in different fields of human endeavor and express their respective potentials fully and properly. Side by side they should develop their physical abilities and skills, develop their feelings in the right direction and learn to control passions and self-destructive emotions etc. They should become wiser and wiser and abler and abler. On the other hand indulging in fleeting pleasures of the senses which titillate (the nerves) and fritter away their energy will hamper their capacity to improve. If we run after enjoyments, we shall not have the power to improve ourselves and those enjoyments will also slip away from us like shadows, but if we continually struggle for self-improvement then happiness will follow us. Of course, we must have some enjoyments or pleasures in a planned and disciplined way

so that we become ‘re-freshed’ when we are fatigued by the constant struggle for improvement and that is why these types of activities are called ‘recreation’ which is an essential part of the science of struggle for improvement which is called ‘education’. And of course we can derive abundant pleasures from creative cultural activities, along with games and sports and useful hobbies. So we find some students engaged in ‘meditation and long prayers’ and yet coming up very well in their studies and some others using meditation and ‘short’ prayers to improve their power of self-discipline, peace of mind and concentration so that they do their studies easily and successfully. It all depends on individual ‘temperament’, but the important point is to be aware of the Goal of life which is not only to be a really well-developed man or woman in whom all available faculties are properly used and groomed, but also to go towards becoming like God.

q: Does one have to think of the society every time he wants to do something ?
a: There are two basic tendencies in the human mind -- the lure of enjoyment and the struggle for improvement. These are also called the pull of the ‘pleasurable’ and the pull of the ‘ultimately beneficial’. If the first pull is left unchecked it leads to ultimate ruination, while the second pull or struggle if checked will stagnate our life. Thinking of society is useful to check the downslide of life resulting from the first temptation. On the other hand, if one is absolutely sure that one is trying to improve oneself then he/she should not allow himself/herself to be checked by society. It is of course always useful to get one’s course of action approved by some really wise person.

q: What is the importance of good behavior?
Is culture to be shown to everyone or it is enough if we have it in us ?
a: We must first understand the subtle difference between character and conduct or behaviour. Character is what we really are ourselves and conduct is how we appear to others. If character is perfect it reflects in good behavior. Otherwise good behavior can also be a ‘mask’. In any case the effect of good behavior is that others become pleased. The effect on ourselves varies -- (i) If it is an expression of good character, then good behavior strengthens it. (ii) If behavior is only a mask, then it may make our life artificial.

Similarly, if we really have the culture in us, it will come out even in our dealing with others. Hence if it is not coming out in that manner, we should know that we do not have it fully developed in us as yet, and hence we must strive hard to develop it more and more on the inside. On the other hand if we try to show or are merely taught to show culture to everyone without really having it in ourselves, we are likely to turn into hypocrites and will never be at ease with ourselves nor with others.

q: What is a friend? Why does the human heart wish to have a friend?
Please give guidelines for being a friend.
a: This is an extremely important question in actual life of any individual human being.
(a) ‘A friend in need is a friend indeed’ is the old proverb.

(b) Really ‘God’ alone is our best friend. The great sage Shankaracharya says that a ‘friend’ is a ‘friend’ usually only so long as we are nice to him, but God is our friend always and ever. (Commentary on Gita 9,18)

(c) This God, who is the Ultimate Reality -- One only, without a second -- manifests Himself in innumerably unique ways through the infinite variety of human beings created by Him out of Himself. This leads to a situation where each individual finds himself/herself different from others, separate from others, limited, and hence, to complete himself/herself, he/she craves for a friend who is an expression of the same common Reality and yet is differently constituted. So much so that many of us feel totally at a loss to cope up with life without a proper friend or friends.
(d) If we can be always aware that friendship is based on two factors -- variety outside, and yet sharing the common background and support of same Universal Reality called God so that the third
friend God is always available in case of our falling out with each other due to misunderstandings etc. -
- we can be true friends always.

(e) The purpose of friendship is to compliment and supplement each other and help each other to strive for perfection. When perfection is reached we are not in need of anyone to help us, and then we can be real friends because we really feel the same God in us and in others.
(f) Friendship should be based on giving and not expecting.
(g) Friendship should lead to more and more improvement together. It should never be against anybody and never lead to common disaster by doing anything bad together!
(h) Friendship is destroyed by imposing and expecting. It is really built up in freedom.
(i) Select your friends very carefully in such a way that every merit in you gets a boost and not the demerits or evil passions.
( j ) Friendship is sustained by each one struggling to be a better and better individual and by always helping each other.

q: What is there in God that we call him God?
a: This question asks us to ‘define’ God. Let us try.
(a) God is Absolute Infinite Undivided Eternal Existence-Consciousness-Bliss (Sat-chit-Ananda).

(b) God is both the efficient and material cause of creation (or projection or appearance), preservation (or sustenance or continuation) and dissolution (or disappearance) of the world. [When a potter makes a pot from clay, he is said to be the efficient cause of the pot while clay is the material cause. In case of the world, God is both the efficient and material cause, i.e. God projects the world from within himself by his own will.]
(c) God is the one Ruler of this universe (nobody has the power to overrule him).
(d) God is Eternally pure, All-pervading, Ever-free, Almighty, All-knowing, All-merciful, Teacher of all teachers.
(e) God is inexpressible LOVE and BLISS.
(f) God is Absolutely Perfect. God is the repository of infinite number of blessed qualities.
(g) God is our Father, Mother, Friend, Lover, Beloved, Support, Innermost Reality, Life of our life, and what not.

q: Why do we respect God so much?
a: (a) (i) We respect anyone for his/her merits or superior qualities. But all the possible merits and superior qualities in all respects are in God to an infinite degree.

(ii) We respect parents and other elders as they are ‘older’ in this world and are supposed to be wiser and know more about the world and about human life than us. But God is the ‘Oldest’ -- pre-existing before the world itself. God is the wisest and knows ‘everything’ about the world and about ‘life’.

(iii) Parents are also respected because they are like ‘causes’ and we are ‘effects’. But God is the ‘Ultimate Cause’ and everything and everybody is an ‘effect’ coming out of God. That is why we respect God ‘so much’, though it is much less than as much we should respect God.

(b) God is also the source of any good merit found anywhere. Hence when we respect anyone we are respecting God reflected in that person. If we know this, we will love and respect God with all our heart and soul.

q: Where is the existence of God?
a: (a) God exists everywhere, permeates every atom; is also beyond everything in his own nature.
(b) God is ever present -- hidingly -- in the heart-cave of every living being.

q: If there is a God, why don’t we see Him?
a: (i) Becouse God is the innermost Reality of everything while we are normally constituted seeing things from outside and require very special training to be able to see the inside.

(ii) Becouse we do not have the needed all comprehensive yearning, One great sage always used to say that God is the abiding reality in all of us. So, some times people asked him, "You say that God is the abiding reality, then why don’t we see Him?" He used to reply spontaneously repeating the same question in a different tone. He used to say -- "What a pity! Though God is the abiding reality, why don’t we see Him?" The ‘meaning’ of this reply is that the question should be asked neither as a challenge nor as doubt but as yearning and pathos!
(iii)Because we have not followed any of the various prescribed methods to do so, and
(iv) Becouse we lack the purity which is absolutely necessary to develop the penetrative vision to see God. "Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God" -- says Jesus Christ.

q: Is it true that God lives in Param Dham (above the sky)?
a: Let us try to understand what is Param Dham and also what is meant by ‘above the sky’.

(a) When we say ‘above’, the crudeness of our thinking makes it appear as if it is something on a great physical hight. Removing this crude idea that in ‘above’ two ideas are mixed up -- (i)’Beyond’ and (ii) Superior -- but both of them may really mean -- ‘inside’. (b) Some people say that God is beyond the 9th ‘cloud’. These ‘clouds’ are the layers of ignorance in our own heart. So beyond all of them means absolutely ‘inside’. (c) Dham means place or location and Param means Supreme, most superior etc. So God lives in Param Dham means God lives in the deepest recesses of human heart -- untouched by all good and bad in the externalised mind of man. Hence Saint Kabir sings: "Lift the layers of the veil to see the most beloved." (d) Let us try to understand in another way. Whenever we see objects outside -- they are located in ‘space’ outside. But when we ‘see’ mental objects like Anger, Hatred, Love, Peace they are located in the space of the mind. But when we directly perceive God who is the very source of all perception -- being the source of our consciousness and who is of the very nature of consciousness, that undivided consciousness itself is the location to see God and hence it is called the supreme sky or supreme space or supreme location.

q: How did people get the idea of praying to the Idols?
Is it correct to worship idols?
Should we believe in idol-worship?
a: Some funny confusion seems to have engulfed the Indians due to modern education, grossness of the mind, and ignorance of the ways of mind.
(a) Let us see what Swami Vivekananda has to say.

It was in Rajasthan that Thakur Mangal Singhji, the Maharaja of Alwar, who had become much anglicised, asked, "Well, Swamiji Maharaj, I have no faith in idol worship. What is going to be my fate?" He smiled as he spoke ..."You see, I really cannot worship wood, earth, stone or metal like other people. Does this mean that I shall fare worse in the life hereafter?" The Swami answered, "Well, I suppose every man should follow the religious ideal according to his own faith."... his eyes lighted on a picture of the Maharaja which was hanging on the wall. The Swami commanded the Dewan: "spit on it" ... The Dewan cried out, "What, Swamiji! What are you asking me to do? This is the likeness of our Maharaja! How can I do such a thing?" ... Turning to the Maharaja the Swami continued, "See, your Highness; though this is not you in one sense, in another sense it is you. That was why your devoted servants were so perplexed when I asked them to spit on it. It is a shadow of you; it brings you into their minds. One glance at it makes them see you in it; therefore they look at it with as much respect as they would have in looking at your own person. Thus it is also with the devotees who worship stone and metal images of gods and goddesses. It is because an image brings to their minds their Ishta (that particular aspect of God which is most suitable for that individual), or some special forms and attributes
of the Divinity, and helps them to concentrate, that the devotees worship God in an image. They do not worship the stone or the metal as such.

"I have travelled in many places, but nowhere have I found a single Hindu worshipping an image, saying, ‘O Stone, I worship Thee. O Metal, be merciful to me.’ Everyone, Maharaja, is worshipping the same one God who is the Supreme Spirit, the Soul of Pure Knowledge. And God appears to all according to their understanding and their representation of Him. Prince, I speak for myself. Of course, I cannot speak for you."

Mangal Singhji, who had been listening attentively all this time, said, with folded hands, "Swamiji, I must admit that, looking at image worship in the light you have thrown on it, I have never met anyone who worshipped stone, or wood, or metal. Before this I did not understand its meaning. You have opened my eyes. ..." (Life of SW.V. Vol.I P.268-270)

(b) And hence says Swami Vivekananda -- (i) All men are born idolaters. The lowest man is an animal. The highest man is perfect. And between these two, all have to think in sound and colour, in doctrine and ritual. The test of having ceased to be an idolater is : when you say ‘I’, does the body come into your thought or not? If it does, then you are still a worshipper of idols. (C.W.of Sw.V.,Vol.8, P.229-230)

(ii) The man who is bowing down before the idol; ... It is peculiar to the Hindus. The man is before the idol, and he shuts his eyes and tries to think, "I am He; I have neither life nor death; I have neither father nor mother; I am not bound by time or space; I am Existence infinite, Bliss infinite and Knowledge infinite; I am He, I am He." ... this he repeats and then says, "O Lord, I cannot conceive Thee in myself; I am a poor man." ... You may take the most learned man you have and ask him to think of spirit as spirit; he cannot ... It is impossible to think of spirit without training. (Vol.8,P 210-211)

(iii) Among the Jews, idol worship is condemned, but they had a temple in which was kept a chest which they called an ark, in which the Tables of the Law were preserved, and above the chest were two figures of angels with wings outstretched, between which the Divine Presence was supposed to manifest itself as a cloud. That temple has long since been destroyed, but the new temples are made exactly after the old fashion, and in the chest religious books are kept. The Roman Catholics and the Greek Christians have idol-worship in certain forms. The image of Jesus and that of his mother are worshipped. Among Protestants there is no idol-worship, yet they worship God in a personal form, which may be called idol-worship in another form. Among Parsees and Iranians fire-worship is carried on to a great extent. Among Mohammedans the prophets and great and noble persons are worshipped, and they turn their faces towards the Caaba when they pray. These things show that men at the first stage of religious development have to make use of something external, and when the inner self becomes purified they turn to more abstract conceptions. "When the Jiva is sought to be united with Brahman it is best, when meditation is practised it is mediocre, repetition of names is the lowest form, and external worship is the lowest of the low." But it should be distinctly understood that even in practising the last there is no sin. Everybody ought to do what he is able to do; and if he be dissuaded from that, he will do it in some other way in order to attain his end. So we should not speak ill of a man who worships idols. He is in that stage of growth, and, therefore, must have them; wise men should try to help forward such men and get them to do better. But there is no use in quarrelling about these various sorts of worship. (Vol.3, P.362-363)

(iv) It has become a trite saying that idolatry is wrong, and every man swallows it at the present time without questioning. I once thought so, and to pay the penalty of that I had to learn my lesson sitting at the feet of a man who realised everything through idols; I allude to Ramakrishna Paramahansa. If such Ramakrishna Paramahansas are produced by idol worship, what will you have -- the reformer’s creed or any number of idols? I want an answer. Take a thousand idols more if you can produce Ramakrishna Paramahansas through idol-worship, and may God speed you! Produce such noble natures by any means you can. Yet idolatry is condemned! Why? Nobody knows. Because some hundreds of years ago some man of Jewish blood happened to condemn it? That is, he happened to condemn everybody else’s idols except his own. If God is represented in any beautiful form or any

symbolic form, said the Jew, it is awfully bad; it is sin. But if He is represented in the form of a chest, with two angels sitting on each side, and a cloud hanging over it, it is the holiest of the holy. If God comes in the form of a dove, it is holy. But if He comes in the form of a cow, it is heathen superstition; condemn it! That is how the world goes. That is why the poet says, "what fools we mortals be!" (Vol.3,P.218)
(c) And what then is Sri Ramakrishna’s final advice? --

1. While raising a building, the scaffolding is indispensable; but when the work is completed, no one feels the necessity of it. So also image-worship is necessary in the beginning but not afterwards.

2. A marksman learns to shoot by first having big objects to shoot at; and as he acquires more and more facility in shooting, he aims more and more easily at the smaller marks on the target. So when the mind has been trained to focus on images having forms, it is easy for it do so on things having no form.
3. As a toy fruit or a toy elephant reminds one of the real fruit and the living animal, so do the images that are worshipped remind one of God who is formless and eternal.

4. You were talking of images made of clay. There arises a necessity for them too. These various forms used for worship have been provided to suit the needs of different men at different stages of spiritual evolution.
5. Why call it an earthen image? The Divine image is made of spirit (consciousness) .

6. Why do these images rouse the idea of mud and clay, stone and straw, in your mind? Why can you not realise the presence of the eternal, blissful, all-conscious Mother (The Supreme Reality) even in these forms.?

7. If a worshipper is convinced that the images of the Deity in the shape of various gods and goddesses are verily divine, he reaches God through their worship. But if he holds them to be nothing better than mud and straw and clay, to him the worship of such images does no good.

8. If there is anything wrong in image-worship, does He not know that all worship is meant for Him? He will surely be pleased to accept that worship, knowing that it is meant for Him alone. Love God; that is the duty nearest to you.

9. When one sees God, one realises that everything, images and all, is a manifestation of the Spirit. To him the image is not made of clay but of spirit (consciousness). (Sayings of Sri Ramakrishna,P.100-101)

q: What is the effect of Mantra (specially Gayatri Mantra) on our body and mind?
a: (a) Let us start with the meaning of Gayatri -- part by part.
Aum = God, the Absolute, Ultimate Reality.
[Bhuh = Earth; Bhuwah = Intermediate space; Svah = Skies]
Bhurbhuvah Svah = The Absolute Reality pervades the earth, intermediate space and the skies.
[Tat = It, Savituh = of the Sun]

Tat Savituh = It is like the luminousity of the Sun OR Sun is the symbol of its self-luminosity. But the sun is the source of physical light while the Reality is the source of awareness and knowledge.
Varenyam = Adorable -- because it is supremely wise.
Bhargo Devasya = The shine of the Self-luminous [as explained above]
Dheemahi = We meditate on It (as the Absolute and pervading Reality and as the source of awareness and knowledge).
Dhiyoyo = Intellects
Nah = ours
Prachodayat = May God, the source of our knowledge, kindle, awaken our intellectual faculty.
(b) In the Indian tradition this mantra was taught by the father to his son/daughter in presence of the teacher who was to take him/her for being educated under his guidance.
(c) If repeated in morning, mid-noon and evening, its effects are
(i) Freshness, vigour and poise of mind and intellect is maintained.
(ii) The feeling that God is my own innermost reality and source of my intelligence and power gives a hold on God, devotion, strength and confidence.
(iii) The repetition of Gayatri or any such mantra representing God increases the power of concentration and memory.
(iv) It checks the mind from becoming wayward.
(ii) It generates spiritual eminence.

q: What are the benefits of meditation?
a: (a) Let us take an allegory to understand, first, as to what is ‘meditation’. During the British regime the administration used to appoint sergeants for night patrolling on the streets of big cities. These sergeants used to carry a lantern each which was shaded on their side. So, in the light of the lantern the sergeant could see all people and all that was happening, and also all people could see each other but could not see the sergeant.

Let us think of such a situtation, now. What could be the different responses of the people involved in it? Most of the people would neither bother to look at the light nor bother about the sergeant but remain satisfied in going about their own pursuits. A few people would feel that they could not have gone about their business without the light, and they would say "Thank you, O light!" and a fewer still would say "Thank you, O sergeant!" without even looking in that direction. Some rare people now and then would look at the light and bow down in that direction. Now, light cannot stand or move by itself, hence there has to be somebody holding it, and the fact that we are not seeing that person implies that there is shade on that side. This is the inference. It is also known from the newspapers that there is a sergeant holding the light -- seeing the people and helping them. So, some one -- different from others -- would be keen to ‘know’ and ‘see’ and ‘talk to’ the sergeant. Hence looking in that direction he would pray, "Sergeant, Sir, will you please turn the light towards your face, so that I can see you? And will you please talk to me!" The sergeant would oblige him if he felt the sincerity in the prayer.

Now, it is the light of God -- who is Existence-Consciousness-Bliss -- which reflects in our minds and in the world enabling us to have this interaction. One feels respectful grateful love called Bhakti for the Source of everything and prays and tries for turning the direction of the light reflected in our soul towards its source. This in short is the philosophical foundation of meditation.

(b) But, there are almost infinite variations in human temperaments, and hence the actual practice of meditation takes innumerable forms -- meditation suitable for each individual is to be learnt from expert guides only.
(d) The ‘benefits’ of meditation which can be enumerated as below -
(i) Everything positive in life grows, everything negative recedes.
(ii) There is a flow of supreme inner joy not dependent on anything in the world and hence
(iii) Mind has a positive outlook.
(iv) It is filled with vigour, strength and confidence.
(v) Is active with clarity of vision, but never restless or out of control.
(vi) Is controlled, steady and steadily active.
(vii) Is concentrated and properly focused.
(viii) Physical health is toned up.
(ix) Memory and power of retention increases.
(x) Potential divinity is manifested more and more
(xi) and, ultimately God is realised, the supreme Goal of life is achieved, man/woman himself/herself becomes divine.

q: How do you define 'Youth'?
a: Children cannot think, while old people have lost the power of action. So youth, in contrast with childhood and old age, is defined as that phase of life when we can think and also act up to our thinking.

q: Is it true of all young people?
a: Potentially, yes. They can think and also do as they think.

q: Do you mean to say that in actual life it is not being carried out?
a: I am afraid not. We seldom think. And even when we think, there is no connection between our thoughts and our actions. We are more led by impulses than by any thinking. Swami Vivekananda said humorously: when a man walks, his stomach goes in front; only in old age, when he is bent, does his head go first. But then it is too late.

q: Can it be remedied?
a: Yes, not only it can, but it has to be, and it must be remedied. i) Every young person should feel the importance of thinking. ii) This thinking should be, to use Swami Vivekananda's words, 'as broad as the sky and as deep as the ocean', and whatever is found, by this thinking, to be really beneficial to whole humanity should be acted upon wholeheartedly.

q: Is it not true that, even if we think and want to act up to that thought, we are unable to carry it into practice?
a: Quite often, yes. But that is because we do not use two more faculties which we possess in our youth; the power of feeling and the power of resistance.

q: But just now you said that we are often led by our impulses and now you are talking of the power of feeling?
a: Yes, they are quite different. Not only are feelings different from impulses, but feeling is different from so-called 'emotion' also. Emotion is mostly biological and leads to 'excitement', while genuine feeling proceeds from the most tranquil heart and leads to constructive steady action. Hence if we learn to feel deeply the conclusions of our thinking, and try to act accordingly, we will have much better chance of success.

q: What is this power of resistance? And, why are you talking of 'chances'? Do you mean to say that even then there is no guarantee?
a: We shall take both these questions together. Swami Vivekananda says: 'A carriage with four horses may rush down a hill unrestrained, or the coachman may curb the horses. Which is the greater manifestation of power, to let them go or to hold them? ...All outgoing energy following a selfish motive is frittered away; but if restrained, it will result in development of power. This self-control will tend to produce a mighty will, a character which makes a Christ or a Buddha.'

So if we develop these four faculties in our youth—broad and deep thinking, genuine feeling that proceeds from a tranquil heart, action guided by and moulded by such thinking and feeling, and, last but not least, the power of self-control, so that the energies are not frittered away, we will surely succeed.

q: What is the success you are talking of?
a: In the words of Swami Vivekananda, 'Each soul is potentially divine. The goal is to manifest this divinity within....

q: How can we practise action and also restraint?
a: We have to restrain impulsive action and practise action guided by reason.

q: Is it not true that the strongest urge in youth is for freedom? Should we curb that?
a: We must analyse and understand what is real freedom.

q: What is Brahmacharya?
a: 'Brahmacharya' has three meanings, or rather three levels of meaning.

Brahman is the Reality Ultimate, which is all-pervading and one without a second. When that is felt, experienced and realized, then one lives in Brahman, moves in Brahman, and has his being in Brahman. This life in Brahman, or living and moving in Brahman, is the primary meaning of 'Brahmacharya'.

In order to live a life anchored in the Ultimate all-pervading Reality, one has to be trained for such a life. This training usually consists of—living with a teacher who is an exemplar of such a life; learning from him the secrets of higher life; study of the scriptures which reveal the nature of the Ultimate Reality; regulating one's life to tone up the body, organs, mind, intellect, and heart; and imbibing moral virtues which enable one to lead a life anchored in Brahman. This training is the second meaning of 'Brahmacharya'.
The third meaning is control of lust.

q: What is its part in spiritual life?
a: Brahman is the Ultimate Reality. On analyzing dream we find that our mind itself takes the form of the objects as well as the apparent subject, i.e. ourselves, who perceive objects in dream. Similarly, Reality is one, but through the mind it appears to be bipolarized into enjoyer-enjoyed. So long as we are engrossed in this enjoyer-enjoyed mode of thinking, feeling and action, we lose sight of the Reality. This bipolarity is acutest in the physical-mental awareness of the opposite sexes, and it covers the vision of Reality.

q: Is it not natural to have this awareness of opposite sexes?
a: It appears natural today, and is common to man and animals. But one who has the capacity to think and discriminate finds that the nature of the Ultimate Reality, of which he or she is only a 'form', is beyond all sex and beyond all dualism, and that sex is a creation of the body-mind complex. As soon as we attain to the non-dual vision of our real nature, we rise beyond all bodily instincts and find true perfection and bliss. A universal love then flows from us, filling everyone around with bliss.

q: But what can be done today?
a: Life should be planned and regulated with a proper awareness of what has been discussed above.

q: Everyone says, 'You are very emotional and immature.' But what are the exact meanings of the words 'emotional' and 'immature', and how to overcome these bad qualities?
a: Let me first mention the meanings of 'emotion' and 'emotional' as given in various dictionaries.
## EMOTION:

1. Strong mental or instinctive feeling such as love or fear. (Pocket Oxford)
2. Strong feeling of any kind; excitement or disturbance of the mind or the feelings. (Oxford Advanced)
3. Mental agitation, excited state of feeling as joy, fear, etc. (Collins)
4. Strong feeling, e.g. fear, wonder, love, sorrow, shame—often accompanied by a physical reaction, e.g. blushing or trembling. (Webster)
## EMOTIONAL:

1. Liable to excessive emotion.
2. Having emotions that are easily excited
3. Given to emotion.
4. Ruled by emotion rather than by reason.

This is what the dictionaries tell. Now let me tell you what I have heard from the wise people: The human mind has three distinct functions— (a) thinking, (b) feeling, and (c) willing. If thinking does not proceed from an absolutely tranquil brain, it is vitiated by our likes and dislikes and a lot of subjective imagination. Similarly, if the feeling does not proceed from an absolutely tranquil heart, it biologically excites the person, and this biological part of feeling is called 'emotion'. In ordinary human beings like us, all the feelings are emotions.

It is only when we attain sufficient tranquility that we are able to remain calm always, and then only emotions are gradually replaced by genuine feelings. Till then we have to apply two forces to avoid emotionalism. On the one hand, we have to practise calmness of mind and self-control, and on the other, we must always temper our emotions by 'reason' based on philosophical understanding of the true nature of things; and also by 'practical reason' based on the experience of the elders. As far as the word 'immature' is concerned, again I am giving the dictionary meanings along with the meanings of 'mature':
## MATURE:

1. Fully developed, ripe, adult.
2. Fully grown or developed mentally or physically; having achieved one's own potential.
3. Ripe, completely developed, grown up.
4. Having reached a state of full natural development; when development is complete; having reached a state of maximum development.
## IMMATURE:

1. Not mature.
2. Not sensible in behaviour or in controlling one's feelings.
3. Less mature than one would expect.
4. Not yet fully developed or grown.

From this it is clear that we cannot 'do' anything to become mature except to try to develop the faculties of thinking, feeling and willing (—will power is developed by selfless work on one side and self-observation and self-control on the other—) and wait for the process to complete itself slowly and gradually.

q: I always hear that girls are emotional and boys are not. Why is it so?
a: About girls being more emotional than boys—well, it is a very general statement and not worth paying much attention to.

q: Over the last few days I was busy preparing for my half-yearly exams, held in the Bachelor of Education course. Yesterday, when the exam was to be conducted, the students went on a strike—simply on the plea that they did not want to take exams. They had put up a petition earlier that the exams should not be conducted, because once our principal had said that on the basis of the marks obtained in these exams we would be given marks in our practicals in our finals, to be held in April–May. Thus the students did not want to be graded now in these exams. Yesterday, when the bell rang for the exams to start, out of 180 students only 5 went in to take the exams. Somehow I could not gather sufficient strength to be the 6th student. Even though I was very well prepared, I somehow could not leave the majority of 175 students.

I do not know if I am behaving like a coward or if I should have taken the exam, thereby pleasing the teachers and betraying the people with whom I have to stay for another 6 months. It was not even the betrayal, but in fact I was so scared to stand against those 'goondas' of my class.
a: Once, when I was in college, the boys declared a strike. I did not resist on the first day. But next day they said that it would continue indefinitely. I did not pay heed to that and went to the college. Just near the college, two or three of them blocked my way and started pleading, arguing, threatening. I did not budge. Finally when they left, I entered the college. One more boy entered unnoticed. The two of us went up to the staff-room and reported ourselves to the teacher concerned, who then came to the classroom and taught us.

The thing snowballed. 'Students' unity' was raised as an argument; we challenged the authority of the 'few' to take decisions and try to force it on all by the slogan of 'unity'. A General Meeting of all the students was called and it was seen that 70% were against the strike, and it had to be withdrawn.

I am not asking you to do what I did, but you should never join a strike unless you are yourself convinced of its propriety and absolute necessity. Where is the question of betraying the students? Did they consult you before taking the decision? Have you not betrayed the wishes of your parents who rightly expected you to appear for the examination legitimately announced by the principal? And have you not betrayed the principal and teachers who were not wrong in holding the examinations?

Considering all the things mentioned by you in your letter, I think you must appear in the remaining part of the examination. Not to do so would be cowardice before what you have termed the 'goonda' element of your class, and a betrayal of the teachers who have helped you all along to learn the subjects. It would also be a disappointment to your parents who have allowed you to join the B. Ed. course as per your wish, though they had other things in their minds. The students who are your companions for the next six months are not going to be of any help to you in your future life, while what the teachers have helped you to learn will be your asset throughout life. And your first duty is to them.
Please take the examination in all seriousness.

q: Am I a coward, always uncertain of myself and depending on someone to clear my thought, my vision?
a: Depending on anyone whom you think to be a wise person for clearing your thoughts, your vision, does not make you cowardly. It rather makes you wiser and wiser.

q: How to give myself up to HER, the Divine Mother?
a: If you force yourself to do what you think to be righteous and side by side be guided by the wise regarding what is really right and proper,—you would reach a stage where you directly feel that you are under 'Divine protection'.
And you have to love HER—the Infinite. Do you have the book, Sarada Devi, the Great Wonder? In case you do not, you should get it from the Ashrama on your next visit.

q: What is empowerment?
a: The literal meaning of ‘empower’ is ‘to give’; hence ‘empowerment’ is ‘the act or process of giving power’. The very idea, taken literally, is presumptuous. You can give power to someone only if you possess it and if he or she does not. In reality God alone has all the power or all the powers gives to both men and women some powers temporarily to use. But in the present world scenario some seemed to have usurped the power given to some others and that is why this so-called ‘empowerment’ has become necessary.

In the Vedantic view, is only a particularized manifestation of the One-without-a-second, Infinite Divine. Hence everyone has recourse to infinite power which belongs to the Infinite Being. Everyone needs to be made aware of this twofold Truth — (i) no one has power of his own — hence this trying to usurp the power is self-destructive; and (ii) everyone has recourse to Infinite power — hence let us make each other ‘aware’ of this truth, and that would be real ‘empowerment’.

q: Why do we talk about women’s empowerment and not of men’s empowerment? Is women’s empowerment different form men’s empowerment?
a: Brahman, the Ultimate, Universal Reality is Itself Atman, the real reality of every individual. It is beyond subject-object split. Everything in the manifested world, which is called ‘appearance’ or ‘apparently real’ or the creation of Maya is essentially endowed with subject-objectness. Russian philosopher Ouspensky calls this ‘subject-objectness’ as “ the irreducible minimum of human experiences”. (When the indescribable ‘fourth’ or Turiya is described as ‘Advaitam’ in the 7th mantra of the Mandukyopanishad, it refers to this subject-objectlessness of the Reality in contrast with the subject-object split in all our experiences in the states of waking, dream, and dreamless sleep.) In this context of the ‘creation’ ‘man’ has preponderance of subject-ness while ‘woman’ has preponderance of object-ness. Without this basic difference there would be no ‘creation’. This basic difference cannot be ignored, nor can it be obliterated except in the state of dissolution of the universe called Pralaya (or in Jnana-pralaya, i.e., the realization of one’s own Reality, which is beyond subject-object split.) This object-oriented consciousness gives rise to Tamas or inertia, dependence on man loke creeper on tree, tendency to receive or accept rather than be pro-active or take initiative, always prompting, persuading, provoking, seducing men to take initiative, be aggressive etc. The foolish women want to be bare-bodied to attract men to do something. (When they do not like what is done, they shout.) Naturally men have usurped all the powers which women have allowed them to usurp. Hence the need for empowerment of women and not of men.

The solution, of course, is neither in ignoring nor in trying to obliterate this basic difference, in but firmly asserting the potential divinity or the real reality — subject-objectless Infinity, the repository of all knowledge, wisdom, love, and power hidden behind this manifested subject-object split. This has to be done by the women themselves and helped by men for the ultimate welfare of the society as a whole.

q: In today’s day and age, what is the real definition of a “smart woman”?
a: Useless question.

q: What is Swamiji’s message for women?
a: Each soul is potentially divine; stand on your own legs.

q: What is the role of women in the framework of the nation?
a: Womanly wisdom; all-forbearing heart. The westerners believe that while men use their reason, women work by their intuition. It may or may not be true, but it shows that women have different type of wisdom than man.

q: Why do fewer women as compared to men come forward to embrace monasticism? Are there reasons both external and internal?
a: They are differently constituted and they can achieve their goal without formal monasticism.

q: Do women require any special qualities to embrace monasticism? [Holy Mother had once remarked that sannyasa is not possible in a woman’s body; again, in another context, she had said that women renunciates like Gouri Ma were basically very manly]
a: Instead of “very manly” make it “more than manly” and you have got your answer.

q: Is women’s nature different from that of men? Is the path to freedom and internal development different for women as compared to men given the combination of social and individual factors?
a: Yes, predominance of ‘object’-consciousness makes them have Tamas or inertia, and also being attached to their own bodies they become extremely attached to their own children which gives them a sort of blindness.

q: Why did Swamiji leave it entirely upto women to decide their own collective future, totally independent of any interference from men?
a: Because ‘man’ can never understand ‘women’ psyche; and also because if they depend on men, they lose their power.

q: From our experiences of collective living in hostels, we know that it is relatively easier for ten men to stay together, but difficult even for two women to stay together — frequent bickering and the flow of a lot of negative emotions. What is the root of this problem? What is the solution? Is the lack of feeling of oneness with other women an impediment to women’s empowerment?
a: Women’ due to their object-consciousness have a slavish mind-set which is the root of suspicion, jealousy and mistrust.

q: There was a change that occurred from Vedic times to the later times of Manusmriti. Education and life-long brabmacharya of women were in practice during Vedic times. Gradually, their education took a back seat and they were being married off early to protect their sexual chastity. Why did this happen? Was this the origin of the shift from soul-consciousness to body-consciousness of women? Logically, are not education and brabmacharya better ways of preserving women’s chastity?
a: Only due to Muslim invasion who saw women only as ‘object’ ( to the extent that they said that women have no souls).

q: How can women change their own mindset in today’s highly materialized age that they are not commodities and objects of enjoyment?
a: The only way under any time and circumstance is the Truth enunciated by Swami Vivekananda — “Each soul is potentially divine.”

q: What are the specific struggle points for women of today? How can they overcome them?
a: The women should themselves find out the struggle-points — then only a ‘man’ can make humble suggestions.

q: What are the special qualities that today’s women need to develop to take up Swamiji’s work of service to the nation?
a: This term “Swamiji’s work”, used mainly in Sarada Math, is strange. Swamiji himself always talked of Sri Thakur’s work’. Any way, the qualities to be developed are unselfishness, devotion, self-control and study of Swamiji’s Karma-Yoga and the Bhagavadgita.

q: When once asked whom he liked better — Indian or Western women — Swamiji said that he liked both, for both have their special qualities. Elsewhere he had written that each nation is a type, and the time has not yet come for the destruction of types, each nation has to nationalize ideas it assimilates from other nations. So, is the road to empowerment different for Indian and Western women — especially in this modern age, when a lot of differences have dissolved? If yes, do the two paths still converge somewhere?
a: Convergence of all paths is only in realization of Brahman and still the manifestations will differ — as between any two disciples of ShriRamakrishna. Otherwise the world will cease to exist when external sameness is achieved.
