q: In what ways can modern women take up Holy Mother as a model of empowered womanhood?
a: The foremost thing is her ‘universality’ — try to broaden yourself in your thoughts, feelings, unselfish action - along with supreme self-control.

q: I would also want to know at some point Mataji's opinion or advice to women regarding self-reflection and self-awareness and how they relate to empowerment. Often in society, it seems like if a woman is engaged in self-reflection and follows her heart in ways that makes the soul happy, it can be perceived as selfish.
a: There is ‘self’-ishness and ‘Self’-ishness, e.g., Swamiji says — “Faith in Self means faith in all, because the same Self is in all. To blind-like eyes, even this may appear as selfishness, but it can’t be helped. One’s self-reflection should lead to the awareness of ‘Self’ which is One-without-a-second’. One should discriminate to find whether the ‘happy soul’ refers to ‘oneself’ or The Self.

q: Another question I have is the role of the rational self and the role of emotional self in building empowerment. Typically in patriarchal societies men's way of thinking has been the hegemony. Women's way of relation based thinking may seem personal and not universal. Often this has been seen as a weaker or "less than" cognitive process. However, if I look around the world women seem to be the ones that hold a society together. So why do we feel so divided?
a: There is a ‘feeling’ self which is much deeper than the ‘rational’ self and far removed from the ‘emotional’ self. “Emotion is biological” — a great sage used to say. He said — “Genuine feeling proceeds from the absolutely tranquil heart. Of course he used to add in the same breath — “Genuine thinking proceeds from the absolutely tranquil heart; genuine will proceeds from the absolutely tranquil heart.” One has to separate ‘heart’ from the emotional mind, though in the beginning the two are mixed. The work of the rational self is to ‘analyse’ which may lead to ‘division’, but if wedded to genuine feeling, it would lead to ‘filtration’ of the pure from the biological. The emotion has a ‘trace’ of ‘feeling’, that is why it holds the society together, but unless it is filtered it leads to ‘war’ often. (Picture showing mind and heart attached.

q: Has anyone seen God in the form of Krishna, Rama, Shiva or is it just the image formed in the mind of people and they are following it blindly?
a: (a) Even today there are many people, I know, who see God in the form of Krishna or Rama or Shiva or ... Ramakrishna , some times even without their seeking to see God in that form. Let us first see some pages of recent history --

"Some time passed that way. Ramawat ‘fathers’ (Babajis) -- men of fervent renunciation, devout and dispassionate ... -- began to pour in. ... It was from one of them that ‘Ramlala’[A metal image depicting child Rama] came to me. ... That ‘father’ served the image for a long time. He took it with him wherever he went. He cooked whatever he got by Bhiksha and offered the cooked food to it. That was not all; he actually saw that Ramlala ate or wished to eat something or wanted to go for a walk or insisted on the satisfaction of a fancy, and so on. ... I also saw Ramlala doing all that. ... As days passed on, Ramlala’s love for me went on increasing. ... I actually saw -- just as I see you before me -- that Ramlala accompanied me. ... On some days the holy ‘father’ would cook food and offer it to Ramlala but could not find him. ... He would then run up here (to Sri Ramakrishna’s room) and find him playing in the room. ... he used to drag Ramlala to his place and feed him. ... The ‘father’ then came one day and said, ‘Ramlala ... has quenched the thirst of my life. My mind is now free from sorrow and pain. ... He lives happily with you and plays and sports; I am now in such a state that I feel happy at his happiness. Therefore, I can now leave him with you and go elsewhere. ...’ saying so and giving Ramlala to me he bade goodbye. Ramlala has been here since then." (Sri Ramakrishna The Great Master, P 526-531) Here everything is objectively real and much more real than the things of the world!

(ii) "The garden-house of Yadunath Mallick is situated to the south of the Kali temple at Dakshineshwar; the Master (Sri Ramakrishna) used to go there now and then for a walk. ... The officers would open the door of the parlour and ask him to sit and rest there for sometime. There were some good pictures hanging on the walls of that room. One of those pictures was that of the child Jesus in his mother’s lap. The Master used to say that he sat one day in that parlour and was looking at the picture ... when he felt that the picture came to life. ... The Master came back to Dakshineshwar temple. ... At last, when the third day was about to close, The Master saw, while walking under the Panchvati, that a marvellous god-man of very fair complexion was coming towards him, looking steadfastly at him. As soon as the Master saw that person, he knew that he was a foreigner. He saw that his long eyes had produced a wonderful beauty in his face, and the tip of his nose, though a little flat, did not at all impair that beauty ... and from the bottom of the Master’s pure heart came out with a ringing sound, the words, ‘Jesus!’ ... When we were visiting the Master long after this event, one day he raised the topic of Jesus and said, ‘Well, boys, you have read the Bible; can you tell me what is written in it about the physical features of Jesus? How did he look? We said, ‘Sir, We have not seen this mentioned anywhere in the Bible; but as he was born a jew, he must have been very fair in complexion, with long eyes and an aquiline nose to be sure.’... The Master said,’But I saw that the tip of his nose was a little flat; I don’t know why I saw him like that.’ (Because that is not what we see in the available paintings.) ... We thought, ‘How could be the form seen by him in ecstasy tally with the actual form of Jesus?’. But we came to know, shortly after the Master passed away, that there were ... descriptions of Jesus’s
physical features; according to one of them the tip of his nose was a little flat.’ (G.M. P.295- 296). (So when the actual person is seen, the photos etc. are left behind.)

(iii) Sri Ramakrishna told Narendranath "... over and over again, ‘God always hears the plaintive prayer of man and he can be seen, heard and touched palpably, being more real than the fact of this conversation of ours. I stake my credit on this.’ On another occasion he said to him, ‘If you cannot accept the form of God or the common well known ideas about Him because they are the products of human thought, but at the same time have faith in the existence of a God, the controller of the universe, He will certainly bestow His grace on you if you offer such a plaintive prayer as this, "O God, I don’t know Thy nature; please manifest Thyself to me as Thou really art".’ ... (Basing upon these instructions) Narendra adopted a new method of practising meditation from that time on. We have already said that in our meditation on the Lord, with or without forms, we can but think of Him anthropomorphically (i.e. through modes of the human mind). ... Coming to this conclusion ... he prayed to the effect; ‘O God, make me fit to see your real nature.’ He then removed all kinds of thought from his mind and keeping it still and motionless like the flame of a lamp in a windless place, tried to remain in that state. ... Narendra described -- ‘There flowed in my mind a current of serene bliss when I kept it still, devoid of all objects. I felt for a long time even after the end of the meditation, a sort of intoxication under its impulse. ... One day, when I was sitting in that condition at the end of the meditation, I saw the extraordinary figure of a monk appear suddenly, from where I did not know, and stand before me at a little distance filling the room with a divine effulgence ... as if he wanted to say something. ... That face has been indelibly imprinted in my heart. ... Very often it comes to mind that I had the good fortune of seeing Lord Buddha that day’." (Great Master P.797-798) [When God incarnated himself as the Buddha, he had practised same type of meditation, and that is why, perhaps, he wanted to share some of his experience with Swami Vivekananda!]

(iv) "... Oblivious of surroundings, the Master (Sri Ramakrishna) one day was pacing up and down the verandah extending east to west, to the north-east of his room in the complex of the temple where he was serving as a Pujari, Mathur (who was almost the proprietor of that temple -- a worldly man, sceptical and yet a devotee) was then sitting by himself in one of the rooms of the separate house. ... The place where the Master was pacing was within an easy range of vision from where Mathur was sitting. ... But the event turned out to be something unthinkable and incomprehensible, for Mathur himself ran up in a great flurry to the Master and started weeping. ... Afterwards ... he said, ‘Father, you were walking, and I saw distinctly that it was not you but my Mother in the temple (the Goddess Kali) over there as you were coming forward in this direction and that it was Mahadeva (God Shiva) Himself immediately when you turned about. I thought at first that it was an optical illusion; I rubbed my eyes well and looked, but saw the same thing. This happened as often as I looked.’"(Great Master P. 433)

(ii) "On 24 September 1926 Swami Shivananda (A disciple of Sri Ramakrishna) inaugurated the building of the new ashrama in Ootacamund. Later he recited this incident: ‘One year I visited the Nilgiri Hills. Learning that I was there, a Muslim doctor and his family came all the way from Bombay to see me. ... He had been educated in England and had a very good practice. He was accompanied by his wife. ... The doctor said to me, "... my wife is particularly eager to speak to you." ... His wife saluted me with great devotion, and disclosed many intimate things relating to her spiritual life. ... She worships the child Krishna and occasionally has visions of him. ... It is her conviction that her chosen deity, Krishna, has been born as Ramakrishna.’(God Lived with them, P.165)

q: How did people get the idea of praying to Idols? Is it correct to worship idols? Should we believe in idol-worship?
a: Some funny confusion seems to have engulfed the Indians due to modern education, grossness of the mind, and ignorance of the ways of mind.
(a) Let us see what Swami Vivekananda has to say.

(i) It was in Rajasthan that Thakur Mangal Singhji, the Maharaja of Alwar, who had become much anglicised, asked, "Well, Swamiji Maharaj, I have no faith in idol worship. What is going to be my fate?" He smiled as he spoke ..."You see, I really cannot worship wood, earth, stone or metal like other people. Does this mean that I shall fare worse in the life hereafter?" The Swami answered, "Well, I suppose every man should follow the religious ideal according to his own faith."... his eyes lighted on a picture of the Maharaja which was hanging on the wall. The Swami commanded the Dewan: "spit on it" ... The Dewan cried out, "What, Swamiji! What are you asking me to do? This is the likeness of our Maharaja! How can I do such a thing?" ... Turning to the Maharaja the Swami continued, "See, your Highness; though this is not you in one sense, in another sense it is you. That was why your devoted servants were so perplexed when I asked them to spit on it. It is a shadow of you; it brings you into their minds. One glance at it makes them see you in it; therefore they look at it with as much respect as they would have in looking at your own person. Thus it is also with the devotees who worship stone and metal images of gods and goddesses. It is because an image brings to their minds their Ishta (that particular aspect of God which is most suitable for that individual), or some special forms and attributes of the Divinity, and helps them to concentrate, that the devotees worship God in an image. They do not worship the stone or the metal as such.

"I have travelled in many places, but nowhere have I found a single Hindu worshipping an image, saying, ‘O Stone, I worship Thee. O Metal, be merciful to me.’ Everyone, Maharaja, is worshipping the same one God who is the Supreme Spirit, the Soul of Pure Knowledge. And God appears to all according to their understanding and their representation of Him. Prince, I speak for myself. Of course, I cannot speak for you." Mangal Singhji, who had been listening attentively all this time, said, with folded hands, "Swamiji, I must admit that, looking at image worship in the light you have thrown on it, I have never met anyone who worshipped stone, or wood, or metal. Before this I did not understand its meaning. You have opened my eyes. ..." (Life of SW.V. Vol.I P.268-270)

(ii) And see what happened in Jaipur. Sardar Hari Singh, the Commander-In-Chief of the state ... did not believe in the value of images, and even after hours of discussion with the Swami remained unconvinced. In the evening they went out for a walk. As they were going along the footpath they came upon some devotees carrying the image of Sri Krishna and singing devotional songs as they went. The Swami and the Sardar watched the procession for a while. Suddenly the Swami touched Hari Singh and said, "Look there, see the living God!" The eyes of the sardar fell on the image of Lord Krishna, and he stood there transfixed, with tears of ecstasy trickling down his cheeks. When he returned to ordinary consciousness, he exclaimed, "Well, Swamiji, that was a revelation to me. What I could not understand after hours of discussion, was easily comprehended through your touch. Truly, I saw the Lord in the image of Krishna!" (ibid P. 278)

(b) And hence says Swami Vivekananda -- (i) All men are born idolaters. The lowest man is an animal. The highest man is perfect. And between these two, all have to think in sound and colour, in doctrine and ritual. The test of having ceased to be an idolater is : when you say ‘I’, does the body come into your thought or not? If it does, then you are still a worshipper of idols. (C.W.of Sw.V.,Vol.8, P.229-230)

(ii) The man who is bowing down before the idol; ... It is peculiar to the Hindus. The man is before the idol, and he shuts his eyes and tries to think, "I am He; I have neither life nor death; I have neither father nor mother; I am not bound by time or space; I am Existence

infinite, Bliss infinite and Knowledge infinite; I am He, I am He." ... this he repeats and then says, "O Lord, I cannot conceive Thee in myself; I am a poor man." ... You may take the most learned man you have and ask him to think of spirit as spirit; he cannot ... It is impossible to think of spirit without training. (Vol.8,P 210-211)

(iii) Among the Jews, idol worship is condemned, but they had a temple in which was kept a chest which they called an ark, in which the Tables of the Law were preserved, and above the chest were two figures of angels with wings outstretched, between which the Divine Presence was supposed to manifest itself as a cloud. That temple has long since been destroyed, but the new temples are made exactly after the old fashion, and in the chest religious books are kept. The Roman Catholics and the Greek Christians have idol-worship in certain forms. The image of Jesus and that of his mother are worshipped. Among Protestants there is no idol-worship, yet they worship God in a personal form, which may be called idol-worship in another form. Among Parsees and Iranians fire-worship is carried on to a great extent. Among Mohammedans the prophets and great and noble persons are worshipped, and they turn their faces towards the Caaba when they pray. These things show that men at the first stage of religious development have to make use of something external, and when the inner self becomes purified they turn to more abstract conceptions. "When the Jiva is sought to be united with Brahman it is best, when meditation is practised it is mediocre, repetition of names is the lowest form, and external worship is the lowest of the low." But it should be distinctly understood that even in practising the last there is no sin. Everybody ought to do what he is able to do; and if he be dissuaded from that, he will do it in some other way in order to attain his end. So we should not speak ill of a man who worships idols. He is in that stage of growth, and, therefore, must have them; wise men should try to help forward such men and get them to do better. But there is no use in quarrelling about these various sorts of worship. (Vol.3, P.362-363)

(iv) It has become a trite saying that idolatry is wrong, and every man swallows it at the present time without questioning. I once thought so, and to pay the penalty of that I had to learn my lesson sitting at the feet of a man who realised everything through idols; I allude to Ramakrishna Paramahansa. If such Ramakrishna Paramahansas are produced by idol worship, what will you have -- the reformer’s creed or any number of idols? I want an answer. Take a thousand idols more if you can produce Ramakrishna Paramahansas through idol-worship, and may God speed you! Produce such noble natures by any means you can. Yet idolatry is condemned! Why? Nobody knows. Because some hundreds of years ago some man of Jewish blood happened to condemn it? That is, he happened to condemn everybody else’s idols except his own. If God is represented in any beautiful form or any symbolic form, said the Jew, it is awfully bad; it is sin. But if He is represented in the form of a chest, with two angels sitting on each side, and a cloud hanging over it, it is the holiest of the holy. If God comes in the form of a dove, it is holy. But if He comes in the form of a cow, it is heathen superstition; condemn it! That is how the world goes. That is why the poet says, "what fools we mortals be!" (Vol.3,P.218)
(c) And what then is Sri Ramakrishna’s final advice? --

1. While raising a building, the scaffolding is indispensable; but when the work is completed, no one feels the necessity of it. So also image-worship is necessary in the beginning but not afterwards.

2. A marksman learns to shoot by first having big objects to shoot at; and as he acquires more and more facility in shooting, he aims more and more easily at the smaller marks on the target. So when the mind has been trained to focus on images having forms, it is easy for it do so on things having no form.
3. As a toy fruit or a toy elephant reminds one of the real fruit and the living animal, so do the images that are worshipped remind one of God who is formless and eternal.

4. You were talking of images made of clay. There arises a necessity for them too. These various forms used for worship have been provided to suit the needs of different men at different stages of spiritual evolution.
5. Why call it an earthen image? The Divine image is made of spirit (consciousness) .

6. Why do these images rouse the idea of mud and clay, stone and straw, in your mind? Why can you not realise the presence of the eternal, blissful, all-conscious Mother (The Supreme Reality) even in these forms.?

7. If a worshipper is convinced that the images of the Deity in the shape of various gods and goddesses are verily divine, he reaches God through their worship. But if he holds them to be nothing better than mud and straw and clay, to him the worship of such images does no good.

8. If there is anything wrong in image-worship, does He not know that all worship is meant for Him? He will surely be pleased to accept that worship, knowing that it is meant for Him alone. Love God; that is the duty nearest to you.

9. When one sees God, one realises that everything, images and all, is a manifestation of the Spirit. To him the image is not made of clay but of spirit (consciousness). (Sayings of Sri Ramakrishna,P.100-101)
Now we are in a position to find answers to all questions on idol worship by ourselves.

q: Is it necessary to offer Prasad to God? How does He accept it?
a: Let us correct our language a little. When we ‘offer’ anything to God, it should be called Naivedya. (Naivedya = offering); it becomes prasad (sanctified food) only after God has accepted it.

(a) God has created the world; God has created everything in the world; God has created us; God has created our capacity to do anything; God has created food; God has created the capacity in us to eat food. Everything is God’s. Everything belongs to God. If we understand this thoroughly, should we not think and feel every time that we owe to God our eating food or enjoying the world or doing things? If we do not, we will be thieves, and our eating etc. will be sinful and we shall be sinful -- says the Bhagavad Gita.(3, 12-13)

(b) If we love anyone really -- do we not feel much more happy by feeding him/her first and then eating the residual? If we do not feel that way, aren’t we too selfish and love our enjoyments more than anything else? Those who ‘love’ God feel that way. And hence they offer everything to God or rather they try to make God eat first before they do so.

(c) Similarly, if you have high regard for some one do you not feel like serving him/her? Those who have highest regard for God feel like this. Offering food etc. becomes a part of those acts of service. All these actions help us to feel the living presence of God.
(d) How does God accept the food offered? Let us read some narration from ‘Sri Ramakrishna The Great Master’ (P.146-147)

" Formerly when he(Sri Ramakrishna) offered cooked food etc, to the Mother (Goddess Kali) he used to see an extraordinary ray of light coming out beaming from Her eyes, touching all the offered articles, taking their essential parts and withdrawing itself again into Her eyes. Now he saw that even before the offering was made, the same Mother sat down to take the offerings in Her very Person, illumining the temple with the effulgence of Her holy person. One day Hriday(Sri Ramakrishna’s nephew) came suddenly at the time of the worship and saw that the Master (Sri Ramakrishna) had taken in his hands an Arghya

consisting of Chinaroses and Bilva Leaves, which he was going to offer to the lotus feet of the divine Mother. He was absorbed thinking of Her, when he cried out suddenly, saying, "Wait, wait. Let me utter the Mantra first, and then Thou mayest take it." He then offered the food ritually before finishing the worship.
(e) There is an independent corroboration with some more explanation in a passage from the "The Gospel of the Holy Mother"(P.101-102) --
Disciple : Does the Master really partake of the food that you offer him? Mother (Holy Mother Sri Sarada Devi) : Yes, He does.
Disciple : But we do not see any sign of it.

Mother : A light comes out of his eyes and licks all the articles of food. His ambrosial touch replenishes them again. So there is no decrease. ... Why? Does the Master require any food? He doesn’t. He eats the food offering only for the gratification of the devotees. The sacred prasad purifies the heart. The mind becomes impure, if one eats food without first offering to God.
Disciple : Does the Master really partake of the food offering?
Mother : Yes, do I not notice whether he partakes of the food or not? The Master takes his seat before the plate and then partakes of the food.
Disciple : Do you then actually see it?

Mother : Yes, In the case of some offerings, he actually eats and in other cases he merely looks at them. Take your own case. You don’t like to eat all things at all times. Nor do you relish the food offered by anyone and everyone. It is like that.

q: Why did Sri Ramakrishna marry?
a: Swami Saradananda, in his ‘Sri Ramakrishna – the Great Master’, has analyzed and discussed this Question in great detail, and from various perspectives, and has come to the unambiguous conclusion that it was for the purpose of setting up a perfect ideal for conjugal life before humanity at large and not for anything less than that.

q: What is this ‘ideal’ that you speak of?
a: The husband and wife are wedded for spiritual comradeship and not for the satisfaction of animal propensities.

q: How did they – Sri Ramakrishna and his spiritual consort Sri Sarada Devi – set up this ideal in a perfect example?
a: (a) One day, while the Holy Mother Sarada Devi was gently massaging his lotus feet, Sri Ramakrishna suddenly asked her, ‘‘Have you come to drag me down to the life of this world?” Out came the reply: “Why should it be so? I have come to help you in my own way in attaining the aim of your life.”

(b) It was her turn one day to ask him all of a sudden, “How do you look upon me?” He replied without hesitation: “The Mother Who is in the temple is the same as the one who gave birth to this body and the same Mother in the temple in another (your) form is massaging my feet.”

q: What is the significance of this last statement?
a: It means that throughout he had maintained the ‘mother-consciousness’ towards all women.

q: How did the Holy Mother help him in her own way?
a: By serving him wholeheartedly without expecting anything whatsoever from him.

q: How could she do so?
a: She says, “From the time of my first meeting with him (when she was about 13 years of age) at Kamarpukur, I felt, and I continuously feel since then, that a pitcher full of Bliss has been kept in my Heart.” ‘Pitcher full of Bliss in the Heart’ symbolically means ‘the Heart overflowing with spontaneity of nectarial bliss’. In such a state why will she ‘expect’ anything? She would rather serve him with her whole soul, not as a ‘duty’ but as a natural outcome of this joy which has come due to his mere presence as it were.

q: Did everyone who come near him feel like that?
a: Yes and no. According to the purity of each one’s heart he or she would feel this spiritual bliss to that degree or extent.

q: Does it mean that the Holy Mother Sarada was pre-eminently suited to receive the spirituality and pure bliss overflowing from Sri Ramakrishna?
a: Certainly so. It was during Sri Ramakrishna’s stay in his native place Kamarpukur. He had already accepted the position of a worshipper in the Kali temple at Dakshineswar near Calcutta. Through that worship, he had fully merged himself in the divinity of Mother Kali- the source of the entire creation. His behavior was becoming unintelligible to ordinary mortals who are mad after some worldly pursuit or other. It is these ‘normal’ people maddened by their worldly pursuits who think that a superconscious person is ‘abnormal’ or insane. This is why he was taken to his native village where his mother and elder brother watched him with attention and care. When his supernormal consciousness became digested as it were, they thought that he had come down to normalcy. They wanted to chain him down to this normalcy by arranging his marriage so that he might not be able to soar high again! But they were doing it secretly as they thought that he might oppose the idea. They were not aware of the mission for which he was born on earth. It was during these days that he gave out the ecstatic utterance: “It is futile to search here and there, for, the bride has been earmarked and you will find her in Sri Ramachandra Mukherji’s house in the village of Jayrambati.’’ Jayrambati is just two miles away from Kamarpukur and it was here that they actually found her – our Holy Mother Sarada!

q: Did the Holy Mother herself know about the divine mission to be fulfilled by her marriage with Sri Bhagavan Ramakrishna?
a: The villagers do say such a thing. Once in the village of Sihar, which is near Kamarpukur and Jayrambati, There was a festive gathering. Sarada was just an infant girl then and sitting on the lap of a lady. They asked her in jest whom she would like to marry and she pointed her small hands to wards Gadadhar, as Sri Ramakrishna was then known, sitting in the men’s wing!

q: Can we not have any human, non-mystic indication of the supreme fitness of their union?
a: Let us try to analyze their respective mental make-up or innermost constitution. Superconscious wisdom, absolute and palpable renunciation, purity – this is what Sri Bhagavan Ramakrishna represents to us. And Mother? Once when she found some of the girls taking on vain matters, she immediately changed the drift of their talk by posing a question: “Yes, dear ones, tell me – what should one pray for from God?” The girls, who thought much of their intelligence, started declaring: “Why? One should pray for all the good things of life”, “One should ask for merits of character”, “and intelligence”; “and devotion” etc. etc. A little while afterwards, they discovered that having given a new drift to their talks and thoughts she was keeping quiet and to herself as it were. “But Auntie.” asked some of them, “You have not told us your opinion of what one should ask for from God!” Then she spoke out her innermost thoughts; her very being was expressed in words when she said, “To me the only thing one should pray for is desirelessness” This is Sarada – unerring judgment, most natural noncovetousness and crystal purity. And what sort of purity?

q: Yes, please tell us something about her purity.
a: Looking at the full moon on a bright night she would pray: “Lord, even this divine moon has spots on it; may not my mind have even the least spot of impurity in it.” What an Idea! And the fantastic purity and originality of the mind of Sarada which conceived this idea! Nothing, even a small fraction, less than full cent-per-cent purity, is acceptable to such a personality. This is what makes her pre-eminently fit to share the divine mission of Sri Ramakrishna – The blazing fire of pure renunciation. Swami Abhedananda pays homage to Sarada Devi in the blessed verse:
Pavitram caritam yasyah Pavitram jivanam tatha
Pavitrata svarupinyai tasyai kurmo namo namah
“We bow down again and again to her whose character is pure, whose life is pure and who is the very embodiment of purity.”

q: Would you narrate some incidents where the words and actions of Sri Bhagavan Ramakrishna and his consort Sarada Devi have been complementary to each other?
a: Beautiful question indeed! Smt Aghormani Devi, Who was known as ‘Gopala’s mother’ on account of her constant realization and various experiences of God in the form of the child Gopalakrishna, was highly praised for her devotion by Bhagavan Sri Ramakrishna himself and was equally respected by all the devotees and Sadhakas who knew her. Once, when Bhagavan Sri Ramakrishna was on a visit to the house of a great devotee Sriyut Balaram Basu, during festivities, he had her invited there for participating in the spiritual joy so that the members of that family and others might derive inspiration from her holy company. Balaram Basu’s devout wife and others loaded her with presents on account of their high respect for her and a bundle of these articles was kept in the boat which Sri Ramakrishna and others including ‘Gopala’s mother’ boarded for their return journey. On enquiry, Sri Ramakrishna came to know of the presents offered and accepted and then being carried away to her own house by ‘Gopala’s mother’. The Emperor of the empire of total renunciation that he was, it was too much for him to bear and, though he did not say a word to her, he went on looking at that bundle in such a way as if it were the most loathsome object in the world. He also started talking of renunciation and utter dependence on God and said ,”One who can come away empty-handed from the place visited by him can sit reclining with God Himself as his supporting pillow,” and so on and so forth. ‘Gopala’s mother’ understood it all and somehow controlled her own reaction all along, though she felt like throwing away the entire bundle into the Ganges. However, on reaching Dakshineswar temple, she went straight to the room where the Holy Mother lived and plaintively said to her: “Oh Daughter-in-law, (since she had realized Sri Ramakrishna himself as her child Krishna, naturally his consort was her daughter-in-law towards whom she had a unique love and for whose judgment great regard) Gopala is upset to see this bundle; shall I throw it away?” The holy Mother, the embodiment of compassion, replied: “Why, mother, have you not accepted these things only because you needed them? And who else is there to give you things so necessary for life?“

q: Is this advice not contrary to Sri Ramakrishna’s attitude?
a: Not at all.

q: Why
a: Judging from the results. ‘Gpala’s mother’, being thus consoled and advised by the supremely revered Holy Mother, took only one or two articles which were really essential and distributed the rest on the spot to others and then, cooking a dish or two with her own hands, offered the food to Sri Ramakrishna who also accepted it with satisfaction and was highly pleased to see the result of the whole episode. Thus we see that the actions and advices of Sri Ramakrishna and Sri Sarada Devi are harmonius and complementary to each other.

q: How best to describe the relation ship of the Holy Mother with the Master?
a: In the words of Swami Saradananda, the seer of Truth, the Holy Mother is descried as:
Yathagner dahika saktih Ramakrsne sthita hi ya
Sarva-vidya-svarupam tam, Saradam pranamamyaham

“As the burning power of the fire , which is not different from the fire, ever lives in the fire, so is this Sarada, the Sakti of Bhagavan Sri Ramakrishna, non-different from him, and living and moving and having her being always in him.”

q: Can their relation be descried in any other way?
a: Yes! Here is an incident. Miss Josephine MacLeod, the American disciple of Swami Vivekananda, was then living in the Guest House attached to Belur Math, the Head-quarters of the Ramakrishna Mission. Swami Shivananda, one of the foremost among the direct disciples of Sri Ramakrishna, was then the Abbot there. The Holy Mother was living in Baghbazar across the Ganges. One day, when Miss MacLeod entered Swami Shivanandaji’s room and was about to salute him, he asked her, “MacLeod, have you saluted Sri Ramakrishna?” “Yes, Swami,” she replied. “I am just coming from the shrine.” Swami Shivanandaji then exclaimed in a solemn tone, “I tell you MacLeod, salute salute Sri Ramakrishna again; take a boat, cross the Ganges and salute Sri Ramakrishna once more! She was charged with a divine fervor and immediately left Belur Math to visit the Holy Mother. Thus the one who is Sri Ramakrishna is also the Holy Mother, and the one who is the Mother is also the Master (Sri Ramakrishna)!

q: Do our ancient scriptures say something about this relationship?
a: There is the famous conversation between the seer Yajnavalkya and his worthy consort Maitreyi in the Brihadaranyanka Upanishad.

q: What is the highest point reached in this spiritual commingling of souls?
a: Let us see. It is a new moon day – Amavasya. This special day is meant for the

special worship of Mother Kali; it is called Phalaharini Kali Puja – the worship in which all the fruits of actions done are offered to the Mother. Sri Ramakrishna, the ‘Great Master’ as we call him is getting ready for a very special type of worship in his own room at Dakshineswar. A decorated seat for the Goddess has been kept to the right of the seat meant for the worshipper. The Sun has set in the west. Gradually the intense darkness of the new moon night has settled itself. As Sir Ramakrishna’s nephew Hridayaram has to perform special worship in the temple, he has taken leave of his uncle after helping him to some extent in the preparations. Meanwhile, Deenanath, the priest of the Radhakanta temple, has come to help the Master after finishing his temple duties. It is nine o’ clock in the night when the arrangements for this private worship have been completed. Word has already been sent to the Holy Mother to be present for the worship. She has come and the Master sits on the worshipper’s seat.

The articles of worship have been purified and the preliminary rites have been completed. At this time the Master, by signs, asks the Holy Mother to sit on the decorated seat. By this time, the Holy Mother, while looking at the preliminaries of worship, has already entered into a semi-indrawn state of consciousness. Hence, without full external awareness, she takes the seat indicated and sits facing north to the right of the Master who in sitting facing the east. He sprinkles her again and again with the water from the jar along with the appropriate Mantras. Now, after the incantations, he recites the hymns of prayer: “Oh maiden, supremely beautiful Mother of the universe, overlording all powers, open the gates of success and perfection; sanctify this (Holy Mother’s body) and manifesting Yourself in it accomplish everything that is auspicious and good.” Then systematically offering all the hymns and Mantras to the person of the Holy Mother he worshiped her with the prescribed sixteen articles with the direct consciousness of her divinity. Offering food to her, he places in her mouth a bit from each of the food offerings. Becoming bereft of all external consciousness, the Holy Mother enters into the deepest superconscious state of the One-without-a second Reality. The Master also, having chanted the hymns in a semi-divine state, loses himself completely in the superconscious state of Samadhi. Thus, through their respective merging in the self-same consciousness of the Absolute Reality, the worshipper and the worshipped realize their complete oneness and identity.

Let us bow down to this Supreme Reality, One without a second, manifesting Itself through the Master and the Mother – Sri Bhagavan Ramakrishna and the Mother Sri Sarada Devi, for the redemption of mankind.
